are launching the Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity, a centralized directory for discovering and installing third-party and Google-built plugins across the Antigravity App and the Antigravity CLI. Until now, connecting an agent to external systems meant manually configuring Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints, environment variables, domain skills, and custom subagents across individual repositories or local configuration files. The Plugin Marketplace packages these primitives into verified, shareable bundles that you can browse by category and install in a click. Instead of switching between browser tabs to look up a ticket, inspect a design spec, query production logs, or check a security alert, you can give your agent direct, scoped access to the systems where your team already works. As Antigravity continues to optimize for builders, we are launching the marketplace with integrations from partners across software delivery, enterprise operations, data analytics, design, commerce, and security. Here is a look at what each launch partner brings to your workflow in Antigravity. What are the components of a plugin? An Antigravity plugin is a versioned, self-contained bundle defined by a plugin.json manifest. Rather than configuring tools and instructions piece by piece across individual repositories, a plugin packages up to five extensibility primitives that install, update, and toggle on or off together as a single unit. Skills Skills are modular packages of domain knowledge, multi-step procedures, and optional helper scripts defined in a SKILL.md file. While tools give an agent raw access to an external system, skills teach the agent how to sequence those tools reliably for complex workflows such as incident triage, schema migration, or design-to-code translation. To keep the agent’s context window focused, Antigravity uses progressive disclosure: only each skill’s name and short description are loaded at startup, and the full instructions, reference docs, and scripts are pulled into context on demand when relevant to your prompt or invoked via a /skill-name slash command. MCP Servers Model Context Protocol (MCP) server configurations ( mcp.json ) connect the agent to external APIs, databases, and developer tools over remote Streamable HTTP endpoints or local standard input/output ( stdio ) processes. Plugins can declare required user variables (such as API tokens or workspace URLs) or OAuth 2.0 authentication flows, prompting you once during setup in the Antigravity UI or CLI and automatically scoping tool availability to the plugin’s lifecycle. Rules Rules are Markdown instructions ( rules/AGENTS.md or rules/*.md ) that establish persistent guardrails, coding conventions, API usage constraints, and domain standards. Rules bundled inside a plugin can remain active whenever the plugin is enabled or load dynamically when the agent determines they are relevant to the task at hand, ensuring the agent follows organizational policies and partner best practices such as query cost limits, SDK conventions, or read-only operational modes. Hooks Lifecycle hooks ( hooks.json ) execute deterministic shell commands or scripts at specific points in the agent’s execution loop, including SessionStart , PreToolUse , PostToolUse , PreInvocation , PostInvocation , and Stop . Because hooks run outside the model’s reasoning loop and exchange structured JSON over standard input and output, teams can use them to gate or block sensitive tool calls, redact secrets from tool outputs, inject workspace context at startup, or require linters and test suites to pass before the agent finishes a turn. Custom Agents Custom agents ( agents/<agent-name>.md ) define specialized personas and subagents with tailored system prompts, curated tool allowlists, model selections, and command execution policies. A custom agent bundled in a plugin can be selected as the primary session agent for a dedicated workflow or spawned in the background by the main agent to handle focused tasks, such as a security posture audit, log investigation, or code review, in an isolated context window. Plugins to explore Productivity & Project Management Atlassian Atlassian Teamwork Graph CLI is Atlassian’s agent-first interface to your entire work context: Jira issues, Confluence pages, Bitbucket PRs, along with your connected third-party data sources. Developer Tools CrowdStrike Connect Antigravity to the CrowdStrike Falcon platform through the CrowdStrike MCP server to triage detections, research threat intelligence, prioritize vulnerabilities, research identities, and more using natural-language prompts. Business Databricks Connect Antigravity to your Databricks environment so agents can ask Genie for trusted, semantically driven answers, execute queries against SQL warehouses, and accelerate notebook, app, and pipeline development, all governed through Unity Catalog permissions. Developer Tools Datadog Search and act on your Datadog data. Debug production with logs, traces, monitors, and incidents, then trace the problem back to your code and get a suggested fix. Productivity & Project Management Dropbox Connect Antigravity to Dropbox to search and organize files and folders, inspect metadata, and turn documents into actionable context for seamless collaboration. Design, Creative & Media Figma The Figma MCP server brings Figma into your AI workflow. It gives AI agents the design context they need to generate code from your Figma files, and lets agents write native Figma content back to the canvas. Productivity & Project Management monday.com Connect Antigravity to your monday.com AI workspaces through the official monday.com MCP server and deliver better outcomes faster and smarter, across every use case. Developer Tools Ping Identity Configure and monitor your PingOne environments without leaving Antigravity. Built on Ping Identity’s AI-first headless identity foundation, the plugin combines the PingOne remote MCP server and bundled skills so agents can inspect applications, users, and sign-on policies while helping you seamlessly build identity into your apps. Developer Tools SentinelOne Query your SentinelOne Singularity Console through the read-only Purple AI MCP server to investigate alerts, run PowerQueries on event data, track vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, and ask Purple AI security questions without leaving Antigravity. Business Stripe Connect Antigravity to your Stripe account through the Stripe MCP server to look up customers, payments, and subscriptions, search Stripe documentation, and build or debug payment integrations. Developer Tools Unity Connect Unity to Antigravity in a single click to build, simulate, and manage real-time 3D development workflows. Getting started The Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity is rolling out today across the Antigravity App and the Antigravity CLI. To explore the catalog and install your first plugin, open the Customizations panel in the Antigravity App and browse the Plugins tab, or install plugins directly from your terminal using agy plugin install <plugin-name> : agy plugin install < plugin-nam e > To learn how to build and package your own plugins for your team or the community, check out the Plugins documentation and the Marketplace guide . Before publishing or sharing a plugin, you can validate its plugin.json manifest and MCP server configurations and test it locally from your terminal: # Validate plugin.json and MCP server configurations agy plugin validate ./ < plugin-nam e > # Install and test the plugin locally from your working directory agy plugin install ./ < plugin-nam e > # Verify the plugin is installed and enabled agy plugin list If you are a technology partner interested in publishing an official integration in the Plugin Marketplace in Antigravity, validate your plugin bundle and submit your details through the partner interest form . candidates.title: Speeding up language models for travel applications
candidates.author: Daniel Zagyva, Laurens van der Maas
candidates.summarizationContent: Conversational AI Speeding up language models for travel applications Two optimization techniques, when combined, can significantly improve a model’s speed and cost effectiveness without sacrificing quality. By Daniel Zagyva , Laurens van der Maas October 29, 2026 5 min read Share Share Copy link Email X LinkedIn Facebook Line Reddit QZone Sina Weibo WeChat WhatsApp 分享到微信 x Listen • 7:25 min Key takeaways Combining knowledge distillation (KD) with the Medusa-2 framework produced a final model (TinyLlama at 1.1 billion parameters) that matched the quality of the 70-billion-parameter Llama-3.1 teacher while running 10 to 20 times as fast. For Booking.com's Smart Filters, the KD-plus-Medusa approach delivered responses 15 times as fast for 99% of queries; knowledge distillation alone closed the student-teacher quality gap by more than 90% and made inference roughly six times as fast, after which Medusa heads added a further 2 to 3.6× speedup. On the two remaining use cases, the pipeline drove a 2.9% increase in user engagement for the AI Trip Planner (vs. GPT-3.5) and 1.4% more "helpful" ratings for AI-generated accommodation descriptions at lower costs than other models. Was this answer helpful? Travel platforms serve millions of daily users by answering questions about destinations, offering hotel recommendations, and helping users plan their trips. In recent years, many platforms have turned to large language models (LLMs) to improve these services. The LLMs give accurate, contextually relevant travel advice thanks to their size: they typically have tens of billions of parameters. Unfortunately, such large models are also computationally expensive, and that expense scales with the number of customer queries. What’s more, such large models can be too slow for web and mobile applications, where a delay of even 100 milliseconds can cost a company customers and revenue. To address these scaling and latency challenges, we explored two complementary optimization techniques. One is a compression technique known as knowledge distillation (KD), in which a slow but powerful model produces training targets for a faster, lightweight model. The other, called Medusa , is a framework that transforms sequential next-token predictions — a common bottleneck in LLMs — into parallel computations. Working with leading online travel agency Booking.com, we applied KD and Medusa techniques to the LLMs that power various aspects of its user experience, looking to improve either latency or cost effectiveness. We focused on three features in particular: The AI Trip Planner: A conversational assistant that must extract travel preferences from dialogue in less than a second (latency); Smart Filters: A feature that converts natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time (latency); Accommodation Description Generation: A feature that produces property descriptions on the scale of millions of listings (cost effectiveness). We demonstrated that combining both KD and Medusa maintains the quality of the best open-source LLMs at less than one-third the cost while running up to 20 times as fast. Our framework ensures that travel platforms or other applications that rely on LLMs can deliver fast, cost-effective, accurate responses in real-world scenarios. We presented these techniques at last year’s meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), where it received the Industry Track best-paper award. LLM-powered Smart Filters convert natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time. Our approach: Medusa plus knowledge distillation Medusa is a framework designed to reduce LLM latency in real-time applications such as chat and code generation. It improves computational efficiency at run time — inference time — rather than during training. Ordinarily, an LLM generates text one token — word or word part — at a time. Medusa accelerates this process by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. Medusa does this by adding prediction modules, called Medusa heads, to the base LLM, one head for each token decoded in parallel. GPU hardware that LLMs run on is optimized for parallelism, so it can handle parallel token decoding with little additional overhead. Medusa offers significant speedups, typically 2-4-fold without compromising generation quality. Knowledge distillation addresses the deployment challenges of large, parameter-heavy models by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models to smaller “student” models. Typically, a teacher model is first trained or fine-tuned on high-quality labeled data, then used to generate predictions on additional unlabeled data. The manually labeled and machine-labeled data are then combined to train a smaller student model, which learns to mimic the teacher’s behavior. The student model retains much of the teacher’s performance but is significantly more efficient, making it better suited for real-world scenarios such as high-volume consumer-facing websites. In our work, we integrate KD and Medusa in a unified pipeline starting with pretrained base models. As in standard KD, we fine-tune the teacher on the labeled dataset and use it to generate predictions on unlabeled, domain-relevant text. During the student-training stage, however, we attach Medusa heads to the student model and train it on the combined corpus of teacher predictions and labeled data. This produces a single compact model that inherits the teacher's knowledge while also gaining multitoken-prediction capabilities. The experiment We chose TinyLlama — a compact model with 1.1 billion parameters — as our student and Llama-3.1 with 70 billion parameters as the teacher. We ran four progressive experiments, each building on the last. We first fine-tuned TinyLlama on task-specific data for each of our three use cases — AI trip planning, smart filtering, and accommodation description generation. Even without further optimization, the fine-tuned models were significantly more accurate than few-shot GPT-4o, confirming that domain-specific fine tuning compensates for their compact size. However, their performance still fell short of the much larger teacher model’s. Applying knowledge distillation — training the student on a blend of human-annotated and teacher-annotated data — closed that gap by more than 90%, bringing the small model to near parity with the teacher. The smaller model size also made inference roughly 6 times as fast, but that’s still not fast enough for real-time use. Adding Medusa heads, however, sped up inference an additional 2 to 3.6 times. We tested two Medusa variants: with Medusa-1, we first fine-tuned the base LLM, then froze its weights and fine-tuned the Medusa heads separately; with Medusa-2, we trained everything in a single stage. Both achieved comparable speedups with no meaningful quality loss, but Medusa-2's simpler pipeline made it more practical for production teams managing multiple models. Outcomes Combining KD with Medusa-2 delivered both gains simultaneously: our final model matched the quality of the 70-billion-parameter teacher while running 10 to 20 times as fast, depending on the use case. For each of the three use cases, we used the pipeline described above to fine-tune a dedicated model with domain-specific data. For AI Trip Planner, we showed a 2.9% increase in user engagement vs. GPT-3.5. For Smart Filters, we achieved responses that were 15 times as fast for 99 percent of queries. For AI-generated accommodation descriptions, we showed 1.4% more “helpful” ratings from users, at less than one-third the cost of GPT-4. With acknowledgements to our AWS colleague Aleksandra Dokic and to the Booking.com team: Emmanouil Stergiadis, Eran Fainman, Ilya Gusev, and Moran Beladev . Research areas Conversational AI Search and information retrieval Tags Large language models (LLMs) About the Author Daniel Zagyva Daniel Zagyva is a senior machine learning engineer at Amazon Web Services (AWS). Laurens van der Maas Laurens van der Maas is a senior applied scientist with Amazon Web Services (AWS).

candidates.title: How Zurich is shaping the future of algorithms, 70 years in
candidates.author: Mariana Rajado Silva
candidates.summarizationContent: Forty years ago, when Alessandro Curioni was a high school student, he was watching the news on Italian television as they announced the Physics Nobel Prize of 1986. It went to researchers Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at the IBM Research Lab in Zurich for their invention of the scanning tunneling microscope , a device that has since revolutionized the field of nanotechnology. The way the researchers talked about their invention stuck with Curioni, but he was even more struck by how they spoke about the lab where they worked: a powerful innovation hub, buzzing with people and ideas. This image stayed with him, and many years later, while working on his Ph.D. in computational chemistry in Pisa, he became aware of the research being conducted at the Zurich lab on advanced computational molecular simulation methods. This was one of the only two places worldwide where unique, groundbreaking work was being done on Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics. If he did not learn these new, more advanced techniques, Curioni reasoned, his Ph.D. work would be incomplete. After talking to his Ph.D. advisor, Curioni came to Zurich. When he first arrived, his goal was to learn these methods for his thesis and leave for California, where the technological explosion of the ‘80s and ‘90s was taking place. But somewhere along the way, this buzzing lab in the middle of Europe, filled with experts in a wide range of disciplines from so many corners of the world, changed his mind. These researchers were attempting to solve some of the biggest problems in science and business, with an eye toward tackling important challenges and delivering meaningful impact. There was no better place to do just that. Upon the 70th anniversary of the Zurich lab, we sat down with Curioni to talk about how he landed there, how the vibrant research ecosystem surrounding the lab made him decide to stay, and his vision for the future of computing. This interview has been edited for clarity and length. How did you celebrate the recent 70th anniversary of the IBM Research Lab in Zurich? We had the great pleasure of hosting two distinct events: an evening anniversary celebration on October 12, and a client-devoted symposium on October 13. For the anniversary celebration, our audience consisted of key figures from the scientific, industrial and political realms in Europe, as well as key media representatives. We had the honor of hosting a number of IBM’s clients and partners, several of them also former IBMers, and even Physics Nobel Laureate Georg Bednorz , who was a member of the Zurich lab in 1987 when he was recognized for his discovery of high-temperature superconductivity. At the anniversary celebration, we watched wonderful video messages by IBM’s CEO and Chairman Arvind Krisha, as well as by the president of Switzerland. Jay Gambetta, director of IBM Research, gave an inspiring keynote, followed by comments from the president of ETH, one of Europe’s top universities. We also held a panel discussion with the president of EPFL (another key Swiss university), the Director-General of CERN, and the head of Deep Tech at Nestlé R&D. Lastly, the president of the ETH Board shared some closing remarks before we all gathered at the Think Lab for dinner. Alessandro Curioni gives the opening keynote at the anniversary celebration on Oct 12. The symposium was designed as a smaller, technology-focused event. We invited many of IBM’s clients and partners, and our goal was to spark powerful dialogue and share our vision for the future of computing. After a keynote by Gambetta, some of our lead researchers had the pleasure of sharing the stage with several of our partners: Bosch, Cleveland Clinic, Dallara, E.ON, JPMorgan Chase, and Threema. It was wonderful to host these celebration events — especially with our collaborators and clients in attendance. Through the many inspiring speeches and presentations we witnessed, I think we all realized how exceptional the IBM Research Lab in Zurich is, how much groundbreaking innovation is being done in the Zurich area, and how we are keen on continuing to shape the world of technology for much, much longer. It was more than 10 years ago that I took over the leadership of this lab. Overall, I have a feeling that I have made this place even more connected to the future of computing, to the needs of the company, and to the overall tech ecosystem — and that makes me tremendously proud. What do you see as the key aspects driving success at IBM Research? The first factor I would highlight is our ability to attract top talent, both in Zurich and beyond. If you take a look at similar organizations — even though a concept truly similar to IBM Research cannot quite be found elsewhere — there is a lot of staff turnover. Employees come and go. At IBM Research, once someone arrives, it’s unlikely that they will leave (unless, of course, they choose to for personal reasons). I would call that a culture of innovation done right: ethical, transformative technological development that follows market demand while keeping skilled people engaged. The second key aspect is the global character of this organization. IBM Research has talent from almost every place on Earth, and our impact knows no borders. Many of our remarkable collaborators are giants in their country or even in their continent — but their reach ends there. IBM Research is a global enterprise. Our ability to marry research with the corporate world is unprecedented, and that makes us unique — and hence able to bring remarkable value to all corners of this Earth. Aerial view of the IBM Research Zurich campus. You’re leading IBM Research’s efforts on Algorithms and Applications. Can you tell us more about the work being done in this area? Algorithms play a key role in computing. One can have extremely powerful, advanced hardware, but without the key layer of algorithms, it is simply not possible to extract trusted value from it. At IBM Research, we are creating foundational algorithms that combine classical computing, quantum computing, and AI. We are focusing on five broad problem classes: differential equations and dynamical systems; linear algebra and Hamiltonian problems; optimization and combinatorial problems; probability, statistics, and stochastic processes; and cryptography. We believe that, by tackling these five areas, our results will cover a large percentage of today’s most urgent challenges. AI and quantum play key roles here — the former provides us new abstractions, and the latter brings us new representations. I firmly believe that the future of computing will be defined by the joint use of CPUs, GPUs, QPUs, and an agentic AI layer for orchestration. The synergistic use of these technologies will lead us to fundamentally new ways of approaching complex problems, and hence allow us to reach unprecedented solutions. What is your vision for the future of computing? Being a computational scientist by training, my dream was always to use a computer to simulate the world and all of its phenomena, from the scientific to the industrial realms. I would say there is no better moment in history to do this. The algorithms we are creating can translate technology into tangible value. We are creating a future where, on the one hand, we can do what we have done before in better, faster, and more efficient ways, and, on the other hand, we can do things that have simply been out of reach until now. For the very first time, we have the ability to create extremely accurate digital twins of our world, both in science and business — and that capability is invaluable. Researching algorithms has always been central to my life, but today I find it is more meaningful than ever. Being part of an organization that is leading the connection between technology and societal value is tremendously exciting. The future of computing looks promising, and I am very proud to keep shaping it at IBM Research.

candidates.title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
candidates.author: Google Research Blog
candidates.summarizationContent: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning October 27, 2026 Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs. Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information. While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting , a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten. Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning. Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information. Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states: Active (wake) phase : The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components. Sleep phase : The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement. While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged. Key components of the sleep process The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming. 1. Memory consolidation In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms: Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters. Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning : On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences. Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ( Levenshtein distance ) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text. Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions. Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement). 2. Dreaming for self-improvement During REM sleep , the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop: Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns. Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability. RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks. Theoretical foundations Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities. For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective. This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge. For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space. Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself. Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning. For continual translation , in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges , and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning. In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4 , and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory. For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations. Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25 , sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance. Conclusion Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting. Acknowledgements This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post. candidates.title: IBM and Kaggle launch leaderboard for Java framework migration
candidates.author: Bridget McGinn, Raju Pavuluri, Advait Pavuluri, Rahul Krishna, Srikanth Tamilselvam, Ashita Saxena, George Safta, Michele Merler
candidates.summarizationContent: ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark) is an open IBM benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can successfully migrate enterprise Java applications across frameworks while preserving working application behavior. Across Jakarta EE, Quarkus, and Spring migrations, it tests whether generated applications build, start, and continue to behave as expected, using both focused workloads and whole applications Modernizing an enterprise application is not a single-file coding task. Moving an application between frameworks can require coordinated changes to dependency injection, persistence, database access, web endpoints, build systems, framework descriptors, and deployment infrastructure. A coding agent can produce a migration that looks plausible, or even compiles, while the application still fails when deployed or exercised against its expected behavior. ScarfBench asks a practical question: Can an agent take an unfamiliar application, migrate it across framework boundaries, and leave behind software that still works? IBM introduced ScarfBench earlier in 2026 as a reproducible benchmark for AI-driven migrations. Now IBM and Kaggle are partnering to make that evaluation easier to reproduce, compare, and extend over time. Kaggle consulted on the evaluation design, independently reproduced and ran ScarfBench on its platform while sponsoring the compute, and will maintain the benchmark as new models are released. The collaboration turns ScarfBench from a published benchmark into a continuously updated view of progress in agentic software modernization. The original ScarfBench announcement described the benchmark design, developer-verified workloads, and reproducible evaluation approach in detail. This post focuses on what the latest evaluation tells us about model-and-agent-harness combinations, where they fail, and how the benchmark is evolving with Kaggle. Evaluating model-and-harness combinations ScarfBench evaluates an agentic system rather than a language model in isolation. Each result reflects a model paired with a coding-agent harness that determines how it interacts with the repository and development environment. The results should therefore be read as model/harness results, not as measurements of the underlying model alone. Across 204 migration tasks, Gemini 4 Argon with Antigravity ranked first on the primary smoke-test metric at 75.2%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code at 70.5% and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code at 69.8%. Ten model-and-harness configurations were evaluated. Rank Model Harness Smoke % All pass % Mean % 1 Gemini 4 Argon Antigravity 75.2 71.1 85.9 2 Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Code 70.5 72.1 82.0 3 Claude Opus 5 Claude Code 69.8 60.8 79.7 4 GPT-6.1 Sol Codex 68.4 62.7 76.8 5 Gemini 3.8 Flash mini-swe 66.0 62.3 77.6 6 GPT-6 Astra Codex 65.4 61.4 75.4 7 Qwen 3.8 Max qwen-code 63.7 59.3 76.1 8 Kimi K3 kimi-code 61.1 50.7 71.2 9 Gemini 3.1 Pro OpenHands 39.5 35.1 50.5 10 Gemma 4 26B-A4B mini-swe 24.5 17.6 30.8 The three metrics reveal an important nuance. The smoke score, the leaderboard metric, awards partial credit and gives larger test suites more weight. On that measure, the Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity combination had the strongest result. But Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code had the highest all-tests-pass rate at 72.1%, narrowly ahead of Gemini 4 Argon. In other words, the Argon/Antigravity combination earned the most partial credit across the benchmark, while the Opus 5.5/Claude Code combination converted slightly more individual migration tasks into completely green test suites. The ranking remains stable under a sensitivity analysis. Four of the 204 migration tasks received zero behavioral-test credit from every evaluated model/harness combination. Excluding those four tasks raised the absolute scores but did not change the ordering at the top: Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity scored 79.4%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code at 74.5% and Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code at 73.7%. This result suggests that the relative ranking is not driven by this small set of uniformly difficult tasks. Even the strongest combination leaves substantial headroom: The best overall smoke score was 75.2% across the full benchmark, and no configuration fully passed more than about three-quarters of the migrations. The biggest differentiator is behavioral fidelity, not compilation The clearest result is the gap between code that builds and software that behaves correctly. After excluding the four all-zero tasks, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe each compiled 100% of tasks, GPT-6 Astra + Codex and Kimi K3 + kimi-code compiled 99.0% and 98.5%, and Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex compiled 98.0% and 98.5%. Yet smoke-test scores remained much lower. Across the 10 configurations, compile success among solvable tasks spanned about 25 percentage points, but most configurations cluster near the top, with 8 of 10 compiling 97% or more; smoke-test performance spanned more than 50 points. Among applications that successfully deployed, the leading configurations clustered at roughly 63 to 76% for fully passing tests; Kimi K3 + kimi-code fell to 53%, Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands to 42%, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe to 26%. In this evaluation, preserving behavior was a much stronger discriminator than getting the migrated application to compile. Where agent configurations fail Of 745 classified failing runs, 535 (approximately 72%) were runtime behavioral failures: The application built and often booted but failed behavioral validation. This group included 304 content or assertion mismatches and 210 lost-route/404 failures; 21 were explicit HTTP 500/405 errors. Compile or packaging failures accounted for roughly 20% (152 runs), and boot or dependency-injection crashes for roughly 8% (58 runs). Lost routes and HTTP semantics: In concurrency-taskcreator-quarkus-to-jakarta, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code scored 0/6 after /taskinfo returned “File not found” and a test expecting HTTP 405 failed. In address-book-jakarta-to-quarkus, GPT-6 Astra + Codex scored 2/10 after list and create pages returned HTTP 404. Source-framework wiring surviving into the target: In cargotracker-jakarta-to-spring, Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe retained JSF/JoinFaces wiring in the Spring Boot target, which then failed during startup while creating a facesContext bean. Packaging incompatible with the target runtime: In cart-spring-to-jakarta, GPT-6 Astra + Codex reached a deployment failure because the packaging type left by the migration was not supported by the target Liberty runtime. These failures illustrate why ScarfBench validates beyond compilation: Nearly three in four classified failures in this evaluation appeared at runtime. Agent efficiency reveals different operating profiles On the 200 tasks remaining after the four-task sensitivity exclusion, Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code used the fewest median turns at 32. GPT-6.1 Sol + Codex used 36, Gemma 4 26B-A4B + mini-swe 40, Gemini 4 Argon + Antigravity 42, GPT-6 Astra + Codex 45, Kimi K3 + kimi-code 47, Qwen 3.8 Max + qwen-code and Gemini 3.1 Pro + OpenHands 53, Claude Opus 5.5 + Claude Code 64, and Gemini 3.8 Flash + mini-swe 79. Where harness-reported cost was available — for the Claude Code, Codex, mini-swe and kimi-code harnesses; the Antigravity, qwen-code and OpenHands harnesses did not emit per-run cost — the configurations showed distinct cost profiles: Model / harness Median turns Turns, successful runs Cost / successful run Cost per solved task Claude Opus 5 / Claude Code 32 30 $1.76 $3.83 Claude Opus 5.5 / Claude Code 64 60 $5.98 $10.10 GPT-6.1 Sol / Codex 36 34 $0.64 $1.25 GPT-6 Astra / Codex 45 44 $3.55 $6.65 Gemini 3.8 Flash / mini-swe 79 74 $0.73 $1.59 Kimi K3 / kimi-code 47 44 $1.27 $3.21 IBM and Kaggle are building a living ScarfBench leaderboard The latest ScarfBench evaluation is also the start of a deeper collaboration between IBM and Kaggle. The two teams bring complementary strengths: IBM developed ScarfBench around enterprise Java modernization, while Kaggle brings independent evaluation infrastructure and long-term leaderboard maintenance. The collaboration is intended to make the benchmark reproducible outside its original development environment and useful as new model-and-agent configurations are released. The collaboration has three concrete parts. First, Kaggle consulted with IBM on the rigorous design of the benchmark and evaluation. Second, Kaggle independently reproduced and ran the evaluation on its platform and sponsored the compute. Third, Kaggle will maintain the benchmark long-term and add new models as they are released. The ScarfBench leaderboard provides the public view of these results. Public model submission is not available at launch but is on the roadmap. What we have learned so far ScarfBench was built around the demanding premise that coding agents participating meaningfully in enterprise modernization need to be evaluated on the outcome enterprises ultimately care about: working software. The latest evaluation reinforces that premise. Leading configurations can compile nearly every task in the sensitivity set, but compilation hides a harder problem. Routes disappear, HTTP behavior changes, source-framework wiring survives migrations, applications fail during startup, and business behavior diverges from the expected system. That gap between code that builds and software that works is where ScarfBench is most informative. As new model/harness combinations arrive, a maintained benchmark can show whether progress comes from better generated changes, more effective debugging and iteration, more efficient tool use, or a combination of these capabilities.

candidates.title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
candidates.author: Anthropic
candidates.summarizationContent: Chapter 01 : Case studies Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here . There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more. Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development. So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work. This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer. In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next. Case studies Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more , and see Generate’s technical report . Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more , and see Divergence’s technical report . BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more , and see BigHat’s technical report . Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more , and see Enveda’s technical report . The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more . More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development. “We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.” Michael Pourdehnad, MD , Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy. In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report . Extending our work in the life sciences All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical— that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage. This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out Claude Science , our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing Claude credits for life scientists . We’ve also created the Life Sciences Verification Program to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an open call for guest investigators in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas. We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below. Get in touch with us If you work at an organization focused on drug development and would like to get in touch, complete the following form.

candidates.title: PyTorch opens the AI ecosystem to a new class of accelerators
candidates.author: Peter Hess
candidates.summarizationContent: In October 2025, IBM and the PyTorch Foundation outlined a plan for deeper Spyre enablement in 2026: treating the accelerator as a first-class PyTorch backend and supporting multi-accelerator scheduling. The latest software ecosystem updates deliver on that promise. Together, torch-spyre, Spyre's vLLM plugin, compiler improvements, and continuous integration work are making it easier to bring familiar models and workflows to a different class of AI hardware. AI is increasingly being embedded in the systems that process transactions, detect fraud, analyze claims, and assist employees. And with this growing usage, the AI hardware ecosystem is expanding. GPUs remain central to modern AI, but they are increasingly joined by accelerators with different architectures, execution models, and performance characteristics. Giving developers more choices requires more than building new chips. The software ecosystem must make new accelerators usable without forcing developers to abandon familiar models, tools, and workflows. Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs. Extending PyTorch beyond GPUs At the center of this effort is torch-spyre , a PyTorch backend that compiles ordinary PyTorch code into an executable plan for Spyre. Most of a model’s logic passes through the PyTorch compiler unchanged. When a model contains an operation that the underlying stack cannot yet lower effectively, an adapter can replace it with a mathematically equivalent form that the compiler can handle. The model’s computation remains the same, while its implementation becomes compatible with the accelerator. The move to PyTorch’s Inductor backend also reduced the amount of custom compiler code that the team must maintain. The resulting compiler is roughly seven times smaller than the system it replaced and measurably less complex per function. That smaller surface area makes it easier to carry improvements from upstream PyTorch into torch-spyre and focus Spyre-specific work where it matters. The same principle applies at the device boundary. In a recent demonstration , moving graph construction off the data-transfer path improved Granite 3.3 8B performance at batch size 1 and sequence length 1024 by 9.9% for prefill and 13.6% for decode. Removing that work from compute dispatch as well brought the total improvement to 1.7 times faster prefill and 2.4 times faster decode, with roughly three quarters of the gain coming from the compute path. Preserving vLLM portability Spyre is an out-of-tree accelerator , rather than one of the GPU platforms most commonly supported by AI software. Spyre relies on TorchDynamo to trace a model graph and TorchInductor to lower that graph into representations optimized for the target hardware. Within vLLM, extension mechanisms such as CustomOp and PluggableLayer allow a hardware plugin to customize behavior without reimplementing large portions of the software stack. Preserving these extension points matters as vLLM evolves. Some new model implementations are becoming increasingly specialized for particular models and frontier GPU hardware. To preserve portability alongside that optimization work, the vLLM community is developing hardware-agnostic layers that are isolated from hardware-specific paths and designed to be compilable, extensible, and portable across accelerator platforms. Early support has landed in vLLM, and the pathway has been validated with the Spyre plugin on models including Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Granite 4.2. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, these hardware-agnostic layers delivered total token throughput within 3.4% of the native implementation, measured as the geometric mean across three recent models. One workflow, more hardware choices For IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power11 users, the intended experience is straightforward: Obtain models from ecosystems like Hugging Face and use substantially the same PyTorch-based workflows they would use with Nvidia GPUs. Shared PyTorch extension points hide much of the architectural difference beneath the framework, reducing adoption friction and avoiding an experience limited to a small catalog of specially packaged model weights. Consider an insurance-claims workflow that combines XGBoost models for fraud detection with a Gemma 26B model on Spyre for forensic analysis. The software stack enables developers to assemble the workflow using familiar model ecosystems and framework interfaces, while the hardware is chosen for the work it suits. Spyre's PyTorch integration is also how it connects to llm-d . llm-d runs distributed inference on top of vLLM and is built to support multiple accelerator types, not a single hardware path. vLLM reaches each accelerator through PyTorch: Once a device has a working PyTorch backend, a vLLM hardware plugin can expose it, and then llm-d can schedule work onto it. Spyre follows this path. torch-spyre provides the PyTorch backend, and the Spyre vLLM plugin builds on top of it. As a result, the work that makes Spyre a PyTorch device is the same work that makes it usable in llm-d deployments. Making compatibility measurable Broad compatibility is only useful when users have clear evidence that models run reliably across platforms. IBM Research engineers are building that evidence through end-to-end model testing and continuous integration. This work helps the team detect when upstream framework changes affect downstream hardware support . End-to-end model testing is critical because failures can arise from combinations of operations, shapes, layouts, numerical ranges, and compiler fusion behavior that isolated unit tests do not reveal. Running real models against trusted CPU or GPU references turns each model into both a compatibility test and a probe for hardening the platform. It also gives developers clearer signals about which models and accelerator configurations have been exercised together. In the second half of 2026, IBM, Red Hat, and their collaborators in the PyTorch Foundation including Meta and Hugging Face have pushed new software ecosystem updates covering day-one model enablement, hardware-agnostic models in vLLM, continuous regression and release testing, and native-device integration. A new demonstration on the frontend and backend compiler explains more of the stack . Together, this body of work shows how model adapters, compiler paths, runtime integration, vLLM extensions, and CI/CD combine to support Spyre as a first-class participant in the PyTorch ecosystem. By combining familiar workflows, portable compiler paths, broad model enablement, and transparent validation, IBM is helping make hardware choice a practical option rather than a software integration burden.

candidates.title: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs
candidates.author: Google Research Blog
candidates.summarizationContent: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs October 16, 2026 Pooja Rao, Research Scientist, Petar Sirkovic, Software Engineer, and Annalisa Pawlosky, Research Scientist, Google We are bringing AI agents to the wet-lab bench at Google Research to navigate complex biological landscapes. By grounding agents in physical lab robotics, we can run fast closed-loop molecular design cycles where agents learn how to learn, ultimately discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders for cancer targets. Quick links VERID paper Agentic aptamer sandbox paper Epitope excision paper Share Copy link × Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20 100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency. Realizing this vision requires solving two intertwined challenges: First, frontier models still do not reason reliably about 3-dimensional geometry and physical state — which poses a problem in the automation of the specialized liquid-handling robots that move reagents, track volumes, and execute molecular biology protocols in a wet lab. Second, while agentic hypothesis generation and in-silico design are advancing rapidly, needing repeated cycles of real-world feedback to validate the proposals and navigate vast search spaces, real-world wet-lab experiments have not kept pace, making experimental readouts more of a bottleneck than ever. In this post we share three research projects highlighting our progress on bridging the gap between in-silico AI exploration and real-world wet-lab experimentation: Enabling AI agents to perform safe, resource efficient experimentation grounded in physical measurements by using the VERID framework. Demonstrating closed-loop agentic scientific discoveries on our prototypes for aptamer and de-novo protein design. Grounding agents in physical reality First, we present the VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories (VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory. The safety of a command depends on the live physical context as well as the code. An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible (e.g., lowering an 8-channel pipette into a narrow trough that is too short), logistically invalid (e.g., aspirating from a depleted well), or scientifically compromised by unmodeled fluidic effects. play looping video pause looping video unmute video mute video Through VERID, an AI agent plans, simulates, and executes liquid-handling protocols on a liquid handling robot, combining synchronized multi-camera views with live state tracking to refine experiments across cycles. Built on top of the open-source PyLabRobot framework , VERID provides four core capabilities: Live 3D state tracking: Allow agents to check deck layout, well volumes, and available tips before acting. Fast virtual dry runs: Simulate protocols in seconds to catch collisions or empty wells before touching reagents. Hardware safety checks: Block invalid commands before they reach the robot. Synchronized video and action logs: Capture a complete record of every run for research rigor, reproducibility, and debugging. In our report , we show these capabilities in action through case studies. First, synchronized video and execution traces caught uneven dye stratification caused by dispensing too close to the well floor, allowing the agent to refine its mixing strategy. In the same campaign, the persistent digital twin state allowed the agent to recover mid-run from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting. Second, when the simulator rejected an 8-channel aspiration that physically wouldn't fit in a narrow trough, the agent replanned on the fly and designed a targeted factorial diagnostic isolating a subtle bias caused by residual tip-wall carryover that replication alone would have missed. Finally, in a closed-loop self-play campaign, an agent iteratively designed and ran robot experiments to reconstruct blinded dye mixtures from overhead camera images, identifying its own optical and fluidic artifacts across runs to improve accuracy more than fivefold. Reproducible execution and full trace logs — capturing procedural variables like dwell times, evaporation, and plate layout — lay the groundwork for agents to eventually be able to separate biological signals from experimental noise as they explore and refine many candidates in parallel across rounds. Learning to learn with aptamers Agents need real experimental readouts to refine their hypotheses as computational models do not capture the full picture of what happens in a wet-lab reaction and cannot replace empirical validation. In “ Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery ”, we use protein-binding DNA aptamers to prototype the lab in a closed loop with AI agents over 3 design-test-iteration cycles. Aptamer discovery is a type of experiment common in research efforts for clinical biomarker discovery. A complete aptamer design-test-analyze cycle takes just 7–10 days, as DNA can be chemically synthesized in pooled libraries and read out directly by sequencing. In each round, agents design candidate sequences, which are screened against target proteins on magnetic beads to isolate functional binders, and then sequenced to return rich quantitative data for the next cycle. Agents iteratively design, synthesize, select, and sequence aptamers in a closed loop. Across three rounds on two protein targets with varying difficulty levels ( myoglobin and α-thrombin ), AI-driven rational and de novo design raised confirmed on-target hit rates as can be seen in the image below (to 33.5% and 42.1% for myoglobin and α-thrombin, respectively), though each target required identifying and overcoming a different wet-lab failure mode. On α-thrombin, Round 1 yielded 0% binders because fixed primer overhangs disrupted folding in 48% of sequences; once the agents introduced clamped flanking stems in Round 2 and diversified in Round 3, hit rates climbed to 26.0% and then 42.1% at 98.5% specificity. On myoglobin, as agents prioritized raw binding affinity in Round 2, they heavily enriched G-quadruplex motifs (63% of designs). While raw pull-down increased, the wet-lab data showed that most of these G-quadruplexes were non-specific "sticky" binders adhering to off-target proteins and bare magnetic beads, causing both target specificity (from 75.0% to 19.1%) and true, bead-corrected hit rate (from 10.2% to 3.7%) to plunge. Recognizing this artifact from the Round 2 readout, the agents autonomously revised their design rules for Round 3, capping promiscuous motifs, subtracting bead binders, and pivoting to non-G4 structural scaffolds to recover specificity (72.4%) and surge ninefold in on-target hit rate (33.5%). Across three rounds, agents learn from wet-lab readouts to recover target specificity and improve confirmed de novo hit rates on myoglobin ( left ) and α-thrombin ( right ). In the paper, we also examine how agents reason like scientists, analyzing data and suggesting tweaks to wet-lab protocols, but also sometimes think atypically, exploring sequence spaces that structural biologists might not. Accelerating de novo protein binder design Closing the loop for proteins is more complex. Unlike aptamers, which are chemically synthesized, proteins must be expressed biologically, so each loop adds cellular or cell-free selection, expression, and folding steps. Together with a larger sequence space, this creates bottlenecks on both the computational and wet-lab sides. In “ Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design ”, we applied our workflow to fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) , a large, challenging receptor overexpressed in solid tumors. In just a few experimental runs, the top designs yielded binders with single-digit nanomolar affinity, a level of tight, drug-like binding typically achieved only after extensive rounds of laboratory optimization. Surgical epitope excision accelerates structure prediction 8.6x ( left ), enabling a human–agent hybrid pipeline to nearly double the in-silico hit rate ( top right ) and discover single-digit nanomolar FAP binders in the wet lab ( bottom right ). Computationally, de novo binder design requires generating candidate backbones, designing sequences to fit them, and re-folding the resulting complexes to predict binding. That final re-folding step consumes the vast majority of GPU compute, as it scales quadratically with target length. By surgically excising just the local binding pocket during folding, our pipeline accelerated each cycle more than eightfold without losing structural accuracy. This turns decisions about where to bind and how much surrounding structure to include into tactical levers that LLM agents are well-suited to optimize. In a head-to-head comparison at equal compute, human–agent collaboration, where a scientist sets the high-level strategy and an agent drives tactical execution, nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone while uncovering hits across a much broader range of target sites. To scale wet-lab screening alongside our computational pipeline, we operationalized yeast surface display with fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), a workflow that allows us to screen large libraries of engineered protein variants in parallel by fluorescence. Our next step is to weave these threads together, combining VERID’s fully traceable automation with closed-loop learning for protein discovery to enable agents to directly navigate complex, rugged biological search spaces in the wet lab. Safety In line with Google’s Frontier Safety Framework and our approach to bioresilience , we build safeguards across both the computational and wet-lab sides of our workflows: Safe testbeds and screening: We deliberately selected well-controlled, non-infectious biological systems without gain-of-function risk, as testbeds to evaluate agent behavior and catch drift early. Every designed sequence goes through biosecurity screening. Simulation before execution: Through VERID, agents never send unverified code directly to the liquid handling robots. Every protocol is dry-run in simulation and validated against the digital twin before touching reagents. Human oversight: Humans directly authorize and review designed sequences, verify wet-lab protocols, and supervise robot runs. As AI agents take on more of the design-test cycle, new safety and reliability challenges emerge. Moving toward an autonomous wet lab requires solving these open problems with opportunities for human agency and oversight: ensuring agents optimize for true target binding rather than unintended experimental shortcuts, verifying multi-step wet-lab protocols, and continuously monitoring agent reasoning and execution traces. From grounding agents in physical lab robotics, to running fast closed-loop aptamer cycles where agents learn to explore sequence space, to discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders, these efforts form the building blocks for human-directed autonomous discovery in the life sciences. We're excited by this progress and look forward to sharing what comes next. Acknowledgements This research is led by Annalisa Pawlosky, alongside Pooja Rao and Petar Sirkovic. We would like to thank our co-authors and collaborators across the foundational papers supporting this work: Zach Cutts, John Coller, Rachel Chen, Mathias Bellaiche, Hua Tang, Ryder Easterlin, and Dina Zverinski (aptamer discovery); Jun Kim, Artiom Myaskovsky, Oscar Donosa, Jamie Rogers, and Lawrence Chan (protein design); and Yves Delley, John Coller, Zach Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi Seshadri, Tanner Clary, and Sandy Klemm, with additional technical and experimental contributions from Xinyi Deng, Sanath Ramachandran and Jiawu Bi (VERID automation). We are deeply grateful to Reuven Sayag, Avinatan Hassidim, Ronit Levavi Morad, Yossi Matias, and James Manyika for their leadership guidance and to Matthias Heiler, Burak Gokturk, Bill Jia and Pushmeet Kohli for their support throughout this research. We also thank Shekoofeh Azizi, Andrew Carroll, Philip Q. Nelson, Yishay Mansour, Dan Popovici, and Riccardo Pisoni for their reviews and insightful feedback, Amanie Brik for overall contributions to the effort, and Udi Graff for visual design and graphics for this post.
