candidates.title: Research@ 2026: 10 ways we're amplifying human ingenuity
candidates.author: Google Research Blog
candidates.summarizationContent: play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video Research@ 2026: 10 ways we're amplifying human ingenuity October 14, 2026 Yossi Matias, Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research Today, at our flagship Research@ event, we're sharing research breakthroughs that amplify human ingenuity. From planetary intelligence to advanced medical workflows, we’re putting capabilities once out of reach in the hands of people worldwide. Here are 10 highlights. Quick links Earth AI for public health News from Google collection Earth AI technical report Deep Review blog Share Copy link × We are living through a golden age of research and scientific discovery. For the scientists and researchers at Google Research, the opportunity extends beyond pioneering breakthroughs. We’re also building and sharing robust tools that empower the global ecosystem. AI acts as an amplifier of human ingenuity, creating the conditions for curiosity and rigorous inquiry to flourish. Today, at our Research@ event in Mountain View, we are demonstrating how we put never-before-possible insights and capabilities into the hands of doctors, scientists, developers, public health officials, and others. Here are 10 highlights: 1. Google Earth AI enables planetary intelligence for organizations and society Addressing global challenges requires accurate, real-world planetary intelligence. With Google Earth AI , it becomes possible to forecast public health threats , accelerate clean energy investments, provide businesses with foresight, and more. Today, we’re expanding early access and inviting partners to explore three new ways to access Google Earth AI’s new, experimental capabilities : Conducting deeper geospatial analysis as part of an early access experimental feature in Google Earth . Generating risk assessments and forecasting different scenarios via our planetary prediction engine . Integrating our Geospatial Reasoning agent skills directly into custom workflows via an experimental agent-to-agent API, provides developers with programmatic access to core features like satellite imagery parsing, routing and demographic embeddings. We’re also announcing the integration of Google Dataset Search for querying from more than 100 million public datasets, and TimesFM for planetary nowcasting and forecasting iterations. All these capabilities are powered by over 70 geospatial tools including planetary foundation models like Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) and Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM). They are validated by empirical benchmarks detailed in today’s Earth AI Technical Report . They enable developers, health leaders and enterprise teams to automate complex geospatial workflows. To further support social impact efforts, Google.org is providing $10 million in funding to organizations working on crisis resilience and public health. This includes $2 million to The Milken Institute to unlock infrastructure bottlenecks for affordable housing, clean energy, broadband, safe water systems, and other essential infrastructure. Google Earth AI ’s geospatial foundation models are being used to help predict disease outbreaks and enable public health teams to take proactive, preventive action. 2. Multi-agent orchestration helps scientists build on existing knowledge Existing literature offers a great source of knowledge for driving new scientific discoveries. We built a multi-agent orchestrator, enabling scientists to reproduce previous methods and analyses and then apply them in new settings to tackle important research challenges. As an example, this helped researchers apply a new methodology for solving inverse design problems in fluid mechanics to the design of urinary catheters. They discovered catheter designs that, in simulation, were better at preventing bacterial infections. This complements our existing tools to accelerate scientific workflows. Empirical Research Assistance enables scientists to generate and test thousands of code variations in parallel, and has helped researchers produce results from biology to cosmology to economics. Co-Scientist , built in collaboration with Google DeepMind, is a multi-agent tool that can generate novel hypotheses and has already helped partners, like researchers at Stanford University, uncover repurposed medicines to fight liver fibrosis. 3. Deep Review helps authors improve the clarity and accuracy of technical documents Thorough peer review is a core part of the scientific method. We created Deep Review , an agentic system that provides rigorous verification across complex documents. This is particularly important as AI is increasingly being used to help experts draft technical documents. Many Google researchers and external authors have already used an early version of this system to review over 16,000 research publications submitted to top-tier computer science conferences. It helps with the heavy cognitive lifting by checking logical consistency and grounding facts, while scientists maintain authority over creative direction. Today, we’re expanding access to Deep Review to the general public to help people verify a variety of technical documents from legal agreements to financial reports. System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. 4. Next-gen Edge AI chip enables manufacturers to build the wearables of tomorrow With the rise of wearable devices, hardware manufacturers need the tools to develop efficient edge applications to meet the high expectations of customers for all-day performance. Earlier this year, we launched the first Coralboard from Synaptics , using Google’s Coral NPU accelerator core. It enables AI and ML engineers to rapidly prototype and build devices. Next week, we’ll be revealing our co-designed, next-gen, low-power Edge AI chip, created by Synaptics using our open source IP. The chip delivers greater efficiency and performance for design engineers building the next generation of smart glasses and watches, connected cameras, streamers, and industrial vision and voice systems. The new low-power Edge AI chip from Synaptics, as displayed next to a coin for its relative size. 5. TimesFM and TabFM transform how businesses work with numbers While language models excel with text, business and operational decisions also rely on numbers. TimesFM and TabFM are foundational models engineered specifically to reason over raw numerical distributions — time-series streams (data that changes over time) and structured tabular data (like spreadsheets). Both models deliver accurate predictions out of the box with zero training. They rank at the top of leading public benchmarks in their fields and are available to all Cloud BigQuery users. Today, we are announcing our upcoming integration of these models into Gemini for business . Soon, business owners, analysts, operation leads or coordinators can forecast trends like product sales or hospital bed capacity, based on complex operational tables and millions of rows of data. Sensitive data stays safely within an organization’s perimeter, and people get the answers they need in seconds. TimesFM-3's multivariate forecast helps to anticipate sales lift for a business on planned promotion days in the future. 6. MedGemma enables innovators to build and deploy health AI applications MedGemma , published last week in Nature Medicine , has been downloaded more than 10 million times by more than 65,000 unique innovators. It serves as an open foundation for developers building specialized applications . Developers have adapted it to meet the needs of their local communities, from enabling faster triage in overcrowded clinics to screening for eye disease and cervical cancer . As developers fine-tune MedGemma for more specialities and care settings, we’re pushing the frontier of open health AI. Our latest research advances MedGemma with tool use, so it can draw on available health records and other applications clinicians rely on. We’re exploring new modalities like mammography, ultrasound and electrocardiograms. Early signs point to substantial gains in capabilities, such as answering clinical questions and interpreting radiology scans, skin images and pathology slides. With these advances, we hope to expand what innovators can build, bringing effective healthcare to more communities around the world. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video 7. AMIE study advances the frontier of how conversational AI can support patients and clinicians With our research on AMIE , we’re exploring the use of AI in clinical reasoning and conversations, to understand how it could empower clinicians and strengthen the patient-clinician relationship. Our research this year in Nature advanced AMIE’s capabilities beyond initial diagnosis toward long-term disease management, and in Nature Medicine , we showed how it can reason across multimodal data like medical images and lab results. Our new study in The Lancet offers a promising look into how its capabilities could come to life in real-world clinical settings. At Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center , 98 patients safely consulted AMIE ahead of urgent care visits, and clinicians reported that the AI summaries helped them prepare in 75% of cases. We’re also advancing AMIE’s multimodal capabilities towards real-time video consultations and have embarked on a nationwide randomized study of AI in real-world virtual care settings in partnership with Included Health . AMIE is part of a rigorous research journey going back to our landmark MedPalm paper, and it’s still early days. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video 8. Groundsource makes it possible for researchers to predict natural disasters AI can help us predict disasters with greater accuracy and lead time, giving communities a better chance to prepare and save lives. We’ve been making progress towards our crisis resilience north star : a world where no one is surprised by a natural disaster. Take flood forecasting . Our global hydrologic model , published in Nature , allows us to provide reliable river forecasts up to 7 days in advance covering more than 2 billion people in over 150 countries for the most significant and impactful riverine floods. Yet just one year ago, predicting flash floods still seemed out of reach. Groundsource is our recent AI-powered methodology that turns publicly available information about crises into high-quality historical datasets, allowing researchers to build more accurate predictive models. We first applied Groundsource with Gemini to analyze flood-related news reports and created a structured dataset with over 2.6 million flood events. This dataset helped us overcome a lack of ground-truth data for flash floods and train a new model that can predict the likelihood of flash flooding in urban areas up to 24 hours in advance. The dataset is now part of the Google Earth AI collection and we've made it openly available to help scientists conduct further analysis and research. A global map showing the density of flood events in Groundsource. Red dots indicate floods from GDACS. 9. Learning interactives give teachers the ability to create custom, guided simulations With generative UI, we can go beyond static outputs to dynamically generate functional, interactive software. Our research experiment explores this in the domain of education. We fine-tune generative UI with pedagogical guardrails to enable teachers to create custom, guided STEM simulations tailored to their curriculum. The sample library features over 30 AI-generated learning interactives, all vetted by teachers, for middle and high school physics, chemistry, biology, and math. Schools can sign up to the Google for Education Pilot Program to share feedback. This will help us improve the simulations and develop more for public use, making practice far more interactive and engaging. play silent looping video pause silent looping video unmute video mute video 10. Play with Putty facilitates collaborative, real-time prototyping for teams Play with Putty allows teams to build and prototype together in a shared environment without breaking their creative flow. It demonstrates what’s possible as AI models become more efficient and capable of generating entire interfaces from natural language prompts. People can interact directly with any part of the interface, while multi-player editing supports seamless, real-time collaboration. We first designed Play with Putty to empower our researchers and teams across Google to prototype together — for example, exploring new solutions and visualizations with Google Earth AI. We’ve since opened up the waitlist on Google Labs to bring the joy of human collaboration to teams using AI everywhere. These 10 updates highlight recent progress from our extensive research portfolio across many domains . Technology succeeds when we amplify human ingenuity. In this golden age of research and scientific discovery, the opportunity is greater than ever — to pioneer breakthroughs and share tools that empower others, in collaboration with many. We’re excited about the journey ahead. candidates.title: Putting Earth AI to work: Geospatial agents for our planet's biggest challenges
candidates.author: Google Research Blog
candidates.summarizationContent: Putting Earth AI to work: Geospatial agents for our planet's biggest challenges October 14, 2026 Shravya Shetty, Distinguished Engineer, and Luke Barrington, Product Director, Google Research In a new technical report, we demonstrate how combining domain-specific foundation models, spatial tools, and upfront planning enables a Geospatial Reasoning agent to carry out complex spatial analysis and planetary prediction that standalone LLMs can’t. Following promising tests with partners, we’re also expanding experimental agent access via Ask Google Earth and an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) service. Quick links Microsite Technical report Interest form Research@ top 10 News from Google collection page Share Copy link × When we introduced Google Earth AI , we shared a suite of geospatial foundation models — spanning remote sensing, weather, flood hydrology, and population dynamics — alongside an initial prototype showing how a Gemini-powered agent could connect those models to answer cross-modal questions. Since then, we have evolved a Geospatial Reasoning agent from an early concept into a much more capable, experimental system built for multi-step, geospatial reasoning across planet-scale data and autonomous training of custom predictive models. Today, we are sharing three updates: A new technical report on geospatial reasoning: We present systematic evaluations across four benchmarks, including GeoKTools and GeoExpertQueries, two new benchmarks we developed and are releasing for researchers to test their own geospatial reasoning agents. Our results quantify the value of Earth AI’s specialized tools and planning over out-of-the-box LLMs. Insights from real-world partner testing: Over the past few months, we invited a small group of social impact and commercial partner organizations — including the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa , People in Need , GiveDirectly , the Milken Institute and WPP — to test the agent in support of their own real-world workflows, such as disease outbreak investigations, disaster preparedness, and clean energy screening. Expanding early access on Google Earth and Google Cloud: We are expanding experimental access for both multi-step geospatial analysis and for planetary prediction. We’re offering early access to an experimental deep research update for Ask Google Earth . We’re also providing early access to an agent-to-agent API for developers building custom workflows, including integration recipes for connecting to Gemini . What’s new in Geospatial Reasoning General-purpose LLMs and standard coding tools struggle with real-world spatial problems because planetary datasets are massive, with specialized map and satellite formats that require careful multi-step planning to combine accurately. To tackle complex spatial workflows in practice, our agent brings together four key capabilities: Connected to Earth AI foundation models and planet-scale data The agent connects Gemini to the capabilities of Earth AI’s foundation models — including WeatherNext , Flood Forecasting , the Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) , AlphaEarth Foundations and Remote Sensing Foundations — alongside information from Google Maps Platform (e.g., place information, routing, air quality, rooftop solar potential), Google Earth Engine , Data Commons and Google Dataset Search . Modular skills, upfront planning and a dedicated spatial workspace Earth AI capabilities are packaged as modular skills that the agent calls only when a user question needs them. Before running complex operations, the agent builds a step-by-step analytical plan, selects appropriate fallback datasets when local coverage is sparse, and processes large map layers in a dedicated workspace. This approach avoids overwhelming the agent context with massive amounts of spatial data, while preserving accuracy and tracking data attribution. Every response shows the agent’s plan and the data sources used so experts can check assumptions or substitute datasets. Bring your own data Organizations rarely rely on public data alone. Users can now input their own datasets via the Geospatial Reasoning agent API as CSV spreadsheets, custom map boundaries ( GeoJSON ), or cloud tables. Users can then ask the agent to join their private locations with Earth AI’s global models and catalogs. From multi-step reasoning to autonomous Planetary Prediction Beyond answering complex analytical questions, the agent also powers our recently announced Planetary Prediction Engine . Given a user’s local outcome data, such as regional disease rates, crop yields, or grid outages, the agent automatically selects relevant population and environmental signals, fuses our Population Dynamics Insights and Custom Satellite Embeddings (Google Maps Platform products built on PDFM and AlphaEarth Foundations, respectively) and trains validated machine learning models for spatial prediction, super-resolution downscaling, and forecasting. In our recent public health research , combining these population and satellite signals improved predictions of health outcomes by 12% over demographic baselines and enabled mapping at 8X finer spatial resolution. Our Geospatial Reasoning agent responds to a user’s question by first planning a multistep workflow, then selecting key Earth AI tools, datasets and models that are relevant to the query, and finally executing each stage of the plan in a workspace outside the context window. The answer incorporates multiple Earth AI capabilities into a text, tabular and map-based report. Evaluating a Geospatial Reasoning agent To measure the impact of domain-specific tools and upfront planning on geospatial reasoning, our technical report compares four agent configurations across Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro: (1) a standalone LLM, (2) the LLM with basic web search and maps grounding tools, (3) the LLM with Earth AI tools (such as Remote Sensing Foundations and WeatherNext 3) but without upfront planning, and (4) the full Geospatial Reasoning agent which begins every query with a dedicated planning stage that reasons over available capabilities to assess what it can and cannot do and sets out the stages of retrieval and processing needed to reach an answer. We evaluate four agent configurations, from the base Gemini model, to agents progressively augmented with skills and orchestration that are optimized for geospatial reasoning. The evaluation spans four benchmarks, covering expert-level open-ended analysis, multi-tool orchestration, and community-developed geospatial problems with deterministic answers. CBGB and UnivEARTH are two externally developed benchmarks that test geospatial code generation and question answering respectively. To test agents on challenging tasks that go beyond a single question or use case, we developed two new benchmarks. GeoExpertQueries introduces complex, real-world queries with expert-authored golden workflows that capture analysis best practices in domains like crisis resilience, site selection and public health. GeoKTools contains templated queries with verifiable answers, each requiring correct selection and use of 1 to 4 distinct geospatial tools. Together, this suite provides substantially broader coverage than prior evaluations of geospatial reasoning systems. To accelerate research and development of geospatial agents, we release the development splits of both our new benchmarks in full. Example queries from our new GeoKTools ( left ) and GeoExpertQueries ( right ) benchmarks. GeoKTools tests an agent’s ability to select and use specific geospatial tools and datasets while GeoExpertQueries evaluates reasoning on open-ended, multi-step workflows. Results and key takeaways Two key takeaways stand out from our evaluation: First, domain-specific skills are essential for spatial reasoning. The agent with only basic tools (web search, maps grounding and code execution) struggles on quantitative spatial tasks. Equipping the agent with Earth AI skills drives a significant jump across GeoExpertQueries, GeoKTools, and CBGB. The only exception is UnivEARTH, where even a standalone LLM scores 93.6%, likely because the source NASA articles and answers are available on the public web. Second, upfront planning unlocks open-ended, real-world workflows. While Earth AI skills alone are enough for narrower tasks like those in CBGB and GeoKTools, tackling open-ended problems in GeoExpertQueries requires upfront planning to keep the agent on track across multi-step analyses and prevent it from making unreliable assumptions or taking shortcuts like using web-search instead of spatial tools. The table below shows scores across all four benchmarks using Gemini 3.8 Flash: Scores are 0–100, averaged over three runs. Each benchmark is scored differently, so compare within a row, not across rows. The technical report also discusses limitations. GeoExpertQueries scores come from an autorater that compares the agent’s performance to expert workflows that define the steps an analysis should take, not the correct final answer. We therefore consider the agent’s output as a strong first draft for experts to review and build on, not a final answer. Earth AI in action: Early testing with partners To evaluate how this research translates to real-world challenges, we gave a small group of partners early access to test the experimental agent on their toughest problems. Across public health, disaster response, and infrastructure planning, below is an overview of how they are putting Earth AI into action: World Health Organization (WHO AFRO) & DRC’s INRB : At the start of the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), WHO AFRO’s Emergency Preparedness and Response Hub in Dakar used the Geospatial Reasoning agent to map remote mining corridors where the exposure risk and human mobility are high by cross-referencing forest loss (from satellite images), mining sites (from maps and web data), and population data. In minutes, the team pinpointed 48 exposed settlements and located more than 45,500 at-risk people — a process that normally would have taken weeks. This allowed local responders to proactively deploy mobile laboratories and coordinate border surveillance. Meanwhile, the Epidemic Modeling and Intelligence Unit (UMIE) at the DRC’s National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) used the Planetary Prediction Engine to estimate the risk of Ebola spreading into uninfected zones. By combining mobility flows with historical case trends and Earth AI models and datasets, these weekly insights give coordinators critical planning time before cases arrive. “Mobile populations like miners move faster than traditional paper surveillance can track, creating dangerous blind spots. Earth AI fills those gaps with satellite and mobility signals—moving us from reactively chasing a virus to actively forecasting where it will strike next.” Dr Etien Koua , HIS Program Area Manager & Hub Coordinator for WHO AFRO Emergency Preparedness and Response ( watch the video ) People in Need : Geospatial reasoning helped combine natural disaster forecasts with population and imagery information, shifting analysts’ focus from data processing to providing insights: "The experimental Geospatial Reasoning agent helped us analyze 14 historical cyclone paths to identify high-exposure villages in minutes rather than days of manual GIS work, turning prepared complex data into immediate insights and freeing up critical time for life-saving anticipatory action." - Alonso Gonzales , GIS and Remote Sensing Coordinator GiveDirectly : Teams uploaded custom map boundaries to rapidly calculate population exposure by wind-speed zones during Tropical Cyclone Maila and benchmark tornado damage in Mississippi, cutting crisis scoping from days to minutes inside a single workspace. WPP : used geospatial reasoning to connect Population Dynamics Insights with their proprietary data. Their case study demonstrates how Earth AI insights enhanced the performance of geospatial marketing campaigns, while preserving the privacy of their data. Milken Institute : Pre-development teams used the agent to combine their own lists of 1,500+ candidate buildings with Google Maps Platform’s Solar API and census data in order to screen locations for building community resilience hubs, taking into account rooftop solar potential, mobility data, nearby transit hubs, climate risks, and federal investment zone eligibility. Watch the film Link to Youtube Video Early testing with these partners helped our evaluation and expansion of the agent’s geospatial skills, driving our recent additions of road-network routing, support for larger user-uploaded datasets, and better discovery of authoritative local data sources. Expanding early access: Where you apply to test it Today, we are expanding access across our Earth AI research capabilities to gather more feedback on these experimental geospatial reasoning capabilities. We are making these available to a limited group of early users: Ask Google Earth : preview expanded deep analysis capabilities directly inside Ask Google Earth. This provides an interactive chat experience where you can ask complex spatial questions in natural language, analyze data — including your own — in Google Earth projects, and explore visual results directly on the map. Geospatial Reasoning Agent API : For developer teams that want a customizable, do-it-yourself integration to power custom workflows, we offer an experimental headless Agent-to-Agent(A2A) service. Early partners can connect the Geospatial Reasoning agent to their own custom agents and data pipelines. We provide step-by-step developer recipes for teams who want to connect the service to their Gemini for business environment. Our Planetary Prediction Engine capabilities are also available for early preview — accessible both through an interactive interface for rapid, plain-language modeling and via the Agent API for custom workflows. To express interest in getting access to these research capabilities, please complete our interest form . To be among the first to try out our early stage projects, you can also sign up for our Early Access Pool . candidates.title: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review
candidates.author: Google Research Blog
candidates.summarizationContent: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review October 14, 2026 Rajesh Jayaram and Vincent Cohen-Addad, Research Scientists, Google Research Following successful deployments across 16,000+ submissions at STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR, Deep Review is launching publicly. It’s expanding from deep mathematical and scientific peer review to provide rigorous, grounded verification across knowledge documents, including Google Docs and presentations. Quick links Paper STOC 2026 Blog Post ICML 2026 Retrospective NeurIPS 2026 Blog Post Google Labs Portal R@ Top 10 Blog News from Google R@ Collection Page Share Copy link × Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a validation bottleneck , where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed. Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of Deep Review , an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process. Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences ( STOC 2026 , ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027 ) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool . With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide: Tiered access and scalable API : Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per week. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their Gemini API key for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API. Format flexibility : Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon. Privacy and data policy : Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI. Deep Review accelerates technical validation One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences ( ICLR , NeurIPS , and ICML ) up from approximately 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts. Increase in submissions to NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR between 2023 and 2026. Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans. A proven track record for scientific review Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded. Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below. Statistics and author feedback from the pilot programs of PAT at machine learning and theoretical computer science conferences. How Deep Review works Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline: Document segmentation : The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document. Adaptive budgeting : Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper. Deep parallel verification : Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated. Global synthesis and agentic grounding : A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations. System architecture showing the four-stage pipeline. Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows. Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on: Design documents: Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements. Presentations: Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts. Legal and financial documents: Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence. Deep Review meets Antigravity We’re also introducing the Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern , a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into Antigravity using the Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework . This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the /teamwork-preview command. Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence. Get started We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review: Try Deep Review: Visit the Google Research Portal to review your first documents. Integrate with the API: Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your Gemini API key . Read the research: Read the preprint to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations. Conclusion and looking ahead Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers. Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere. Acknowledgments Deep Review is a collaborative effort across Google Research, Google DeepMind, and Google Cloud. We thank our core contributors and research collaborators — Santiago Balseiro, Taylan Cemgil, Tommaso D'Orsi, Kirk Draheim, Lindi Emoungu, Ayse Erduran, Palash Goyal, Caroline Hartnell, Shobana Kannan, Amy Keeling, Siyi Kou, Bridget Lee, Ian Li, Anoushka Mazumdar, Taylor Montgomery, Mouad Naciri, Uche Okonkwo, Mihir Parmar, Anthony Phalen, Rory Pilgrim, Sarah Presotto Post, Rob Tierney, Drew Tyler, Vishnu V., Vahab Mirrokni, Laura Vardoulakis, Johannes Welbl, David Woodruff, Yunhan Xu, Jinsung Yoon — as well as our executive sponsors Katherine Chou, Corinna Cortes, Burak Gokturk, Vahab Mirrokni, Tomas Pfister, Yossi Matias and the Program Chairs of STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR for their partnership. candidates.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
candidates.author: Apple Machine Learning Research
candidates.summarizationContent: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing content type paper published October 2026 Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models Authors Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter View publication Copy Bibtex Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora. candidates.title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
candidates.author: Apple Machine Learning Research
candidates.summarizationContent: research area Methods and Algorithms conference NeurIPS content type paper published October 2026 The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models Authors Louis Béthune, Victor Turrisi, Bruno Kacper Mlodozeniec†**, Pau Rodriguez Lopez, Lokesh Boominathan, Nikhil Bhendawade, Amitis Shidani, Joris Pelemans, Theo X. Olausson‡**, Devon Hjelm, Paul Dixon, João Monteiro, Pierre Ablin, Vishnu Banna, Arno Blaas, Nick Henderson, Kari Noriy, Dan Busbridge, Josh Susskind, Marco Cuturi, Irina Belousova, Luca Zappella, Russ Webb, Jason Ramapuram§** View publication Copy Bibtex Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities. † University of Cambridge ‡ MIT § Google DeepMind ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. candidates.title: Preparing chip designers for the nanostack era
candidates.author: Peter Hess
candidates.summarizationContent: Earlier this year, IBM announced the world’s first 0.7nm node chip technology . Built on a totally redesigned transistor architecture that layers nanosheets on top of each other, the nanostack overcomes the spatial limitations of packing more transistors into a given footprint. In short, it unlocks the Z axis to reimagine logic scaling for the modern era. The result is nearly 100 billion transistors on a 150mm 2 chip, almost double the density of IBM’s 2nm node chip , with 50% better performance and 70% more energy efficiency, as well as 40% scaling in SRAM memory. Now, as the semiconductor industry approaches this major transition in transistor architecture, IBM is announcing plans to make available an early research and development process design kit, or PDK, for the 7-angstrom nanostack technology in the first quarter of 2027. As the industry stands on the verge of this new era in semiconductor design, the PDK is intended to give organizations an early opportunity to explore how this emerging architecture can change their offerings. A PDK provides the models, design rules, libraries, and other information engineers need to begin designing chips for a particular manufacturing process. IBM’s planned offering will help semiconductor companies evaluate nanostack technology well before it is ready for widespread adoption. Potential collaborators include fabless chip companies, electronic design automation (EDA) vendors, equipment suppliers, and research organizations interested in developing the technology. “We want to invite people to work with us on the early PDK evaluation, and then on codifying the technology together,” said Jingyun Zhang, senior technology enablement manager at IBM Research. Preparing for the future, together IBM’s nanostack chip architecture represents a substantial departure from today’s nanosheet transistors. Instead of positioning n-type and p-type devices next to each other, the architecture stacks one above the other. This approach changes the physical layout of a circuit and introduces new considerations for resistance, capacitance, thermal behavior , and interactions between the upper and lower devices. “The biggest difference is in the device structure,” Zhang said. “When people are trying to design a circuit now, they will need to shift their thinking from how things worked in the previous nanosheet generation, because the layout is changing from 2D to 3D at transistor level for the first time in logic foundry technology.” The first version of the PDK is expected to include exemplary standard-cell libraries for logic functions and an exemplary SRAM design. Circuit designers will be able to use these resources to investigate placement and routing, produce early block-level layouts, and evaluate potential density and power-performance characteristics. The initial release will not contain every model that a mature commercial PDK would include. Instead, it will advance collaborative research, establishing for the first time a foundation for design-technology co-optimization in a technology’s early phase on an open hardware innovation platform. What’s next For prospective partners, early access to the nanostack PDK offers more than a preview of a future transistor. It creates an opportunity to investigate how nanostack technology might be optimized for specific products. EDA companies can begin adapting their design tools to the architecture, while equipment makers can study the specialized fabrication challenges associated with its structure. Researchers can also explore areas such as parasitic extraction, thermal coupling, and device-to-device interactions as the technology develops. “The PDK will help people migrate from nanosheet to nanostack,” Zhang said. “We are standing at a point where we can help the industry get better prepared.” Previous shifts — from planar transistors to FinFETs and from FinFETs to nanosheets — required the industry to rethink both fabrication and chip design. By making an early nanostack PDK available, IBM aims to give companies time to begin that process again, this time with an opportunity to help co-define the technology’s design ecosystem from the outset.

candidates.title: Making AI-driven chip design affordable with open agent factories and distributed inference at scale
candidates.author: Peter Hess
candidates.summarizationContent: As AI systems become more capable, researchers are increasingly asking a practical question: Can AI do more than help write code for computing systems? Specifically, can it actively participate in the design of complex computing systems and rapidly translate algorithms into silicon? New work in AI-driven chip design suggests the answer is yes. But a promising algorithm is only the beginning of a hardware design. Turning it into an efficient chip requires exploring how to organize computation, move data, and use limited hardware resources. Each choice opens up alternatives. Each alternative takes engineering effort to implement and evaluate. AI agents can expand that exploration. Working together, they can propose architectural changes, write implementations, check correctness, and use synthesis results to decide what to try next. The obstacle is cost: the LLM tokenomics for hardware design and the cost-efficiency of design space exploration. A single search campaign can consume hundreds of millions of tokens, and applying the approach across many components and design revisions could require hundreds of such campaigns. A new demonstration from IBM Research shows how open frontier models and efficient distributed inference can change the calculation. Using an agent factory to optimize hardware for quantum error correction, researchers achieved a 52-times speedup over the baseline design in high-level synthesis estimates for approximately $26 in inference cost. Under the same search budget, a proprietary frontier model configuration cost 11.5 times more than a configuration using open frontier models throughout — $299 versus $26, respectively. The proprietary configuration achieved higher speedup (204x), but the open-model configuration established a different result: Substantial hardware optimization can be achieved with a much smaller inference budget, along with the smallest area design. That cost advantage creates an opportunity to apply automated exploration more widely, and to reinvest the savings in finding better designs. The results also suggest that the practical value of AI-assisted chip design depends on more than the best design an agent can produce. It also depends on how much verified exploration an organization can afford. Model capability, the assignment of agent roles, and the infrastructure serving those models all shape the hardware improvements that are attainable within a real engineering budget. By combining open frontier models with llm-d’s low-cost distributed inference , IBM has demonstrated that AI agent factories can move beyond coding assistance and become active participants in hardware design, and they can do it affordably. From generating code to exploring architectures Hardware design remains one of the most expertise-intensive activities in computing. High Level Synthesis (HLS) raises the level of abstraction from register-transfer level (RTL), used in hardware design languages, to C or C++, but engineers must still make countless decisions about loop structure, parallelism, memory organization, dataflow, and synthesis directives. Those choices interact in complex ways. For example, performing more calculations simultaneously helps only if the memory system can supply their inputs. A design that runs faster may also require more hardware resources. Finding a useful balance requires repeated experiments, and the design space quickly becomes too large for humans to explore exhaustively. An ‘ agent factory ’ organizes that work. “An agent factory turns hardware optimization into a coordinated cycle of exploration: A coordinator agent directs parallel worker agents to develop and synthesize alternative designs within a defined search budget,” said Ruchir Puri, IBM fellow and IBM Research chief scientist. When these agents are set to their task, they independently explore optimization strategies. “A verifier checks that the proposed improvements are valid, and the designs are ranked by latency and hardware resource use. Those results guide the next round of exploration, allowing the factory to refine its search as it discovers better designs,” added Puri. Rather than searching for a single solution, the factory investigates many possibilities in parallel, using synthesis feedback to guide future exploration. In the new study, the coordinator planned the search and assigned optimization hypotheses to four parallel worker agents. The workers modified the decoder implementation, and correctness checks and HLS results provided feedback for subsequent rounds. Each configuration received a budget of 100 hypotheses. The agents explored changes with architectural consequences. One transformation reorganized message storage so that the synthesis tool could identify independent memory accesses and execute more work in parallel. Another replaced sequential reductions with tree structures that exposed parallel computation. The value came from connecting code changes to their hardware effects through repeated evaluation. A classical hardware challenge at the heart of quantum computing The key question addressed in the new paper was whether this approach can be scaled cost-effectively using open frontier models and distributed inference infrastructure. To evaluate that idea, Puri and his team demonstrated the approach using Relay-BP, a quantum error correction decoding algorithm, for the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code. Quantum error correction relies on classical computation. Measurements provide clues about errors affecting quantum information, and a decoder must interpret those clues and infer corrections. Doing that quickly, within practical hardware resource limits, is an essential part of building fault-tolerant quantum systems. Relay-BP is a useful test because its repeated message passing is inherently parallel, but the baseline implementation's sparse graph representation and memory-access patterns make that parallelism difficult for HLS tools to exploit. That also makes the decoder a demanding test of AI-driven hardware exploration because the agents must preserve the computation while changing how the hardware performs it. What the same search budget buys The researchers compared three configurations under the same 100-hypothesis budget: a proprietary frontier model as both coordinator and workers, an open frontier model in both roles, and a hybrid with a proprietary coordinator and open-model workers. The open model ran on premises through llm-d. Each configuration explored 100 hypotheses. Costs cover model inference, rather than the full hardware development workflow. All three found verified hardware improvements, but they produced distinct tradeoffs. Open and hybrid searches found useful compact designs, while the proprietary configuration more effectively converted additional resources into parallelism and lower latency. Each configuration was evaluated in one search run, so these results characterize the observed searches rather than establish a universal model ranking. The all-open search also used more tokens: approximately 241 million, compared with 216 million for the all-proprietary search. Its lower cost came from the economics of serving those tokens. This distinction matters for agent factories, where each hypothesis can involve many rounds of reasoning, coding, debugging, and interpreting tool results. Why inference infrastructure matters An agent factory repeatedly returns to much of the same information: source code, design constraints, earlier changes, and synthesis reports. Efficient serving can reuse computation associated with that shared context. The study used llm-d, an open-source distributed inference framework, to support this workload. Its cache-aware routing directs requests toward servers holding reusable context. It also separates prompt processing from token generation, allowing the system to allocate resources to each independently. These capabilities help reduce repeated work and use accelerator capacity efficiently . As enterprises seek to rein in rising inference costs and maintain control of their sensitive data, this latest demonstration showed that open-weight models deployed on-premises through llm-d’s distributed inference stack can dramatically lower serving costs while still discovering valuable hardware optimizations. For the chip-design workload, the paper reports a prefix-cache hit rate of approximately 98% and a blended serving cost of about $0.11 per million tokens. The deployment served the factory alongside other agent workloads on shared infrastructure. Open weights also allowed the team to run the model on premises and retain control over the design artifacts processed by those agents. The cost advantage therefore reflects the combination of an open model and an efficient serving system. Both contribute to making sustained exploration affordable. What’s next: Turning lower cost into better designs Lower inference cost creates room for additional search, but spending more does not automatically produce proportionate improvements. Extending the all-open campaign from 100 to 200 hypotheses increased its speedup from 52× to 60×. The gains continued, but they diminished. The next step is to improve how the agent factory uses that additional budget. Future work will explore adaptive allocation of resources, a wider range of architectural hypotheses, and selective use of stronger models for difficult transformations or search coordination. The aim is to navigate the cost–quality tradeoff deliberately: deciding where additional reasoning, a different model, or a new architectural direction is most likely to improve the design. Evaluation will also need to account for synthesis and verification costs alongside inference. Lowering one part of the workflow is most valuable when the complete process can support the additional exploration it enables. AI for chip design connects two forms of progress into a reciprocal relationship: Better hardware enables more capable AI, and more capable AI can help engineers develop better hardware. Cost-efficient agent factories make that relationship more practical. By making each search more affordable, open models and distributed inference create room to test more ideas and, with better search strategies, turn that opportunity into better chips.

candidates.title: Gemini 4 Argon in Google Antigravity
candidates.author: The Antigravity Team
candidates.summarizationContent: 0:00 / 0:00 Gemini 4 Argon in Google Antigravity The Antigravity Team · Oct 13, 2026 · 6 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Since the beginning, we built Google Antigravity for an agent-first future, designing foundational primitives that would scale alongside model intelligence. With Gemini 4 Argon, the agent-first experience truly comes to life in the Antigravity app. Earlier this month, we introduced Gemini 4 Argon, our latest model with frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense. Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Argon directly inside Google Antigravity for Google AI Ultra subscribers — available in the Antigravity desktop app and the Antigravity CLI. For businesses , Gemini 4 Argon is available via the API in Gemini platform and within Antigravity on eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions. While Argon is designed to tackle your hardest problems, we’re equally excited about future models that can be used as everyday drivers for an even broader range of builders. Accelerating development across Google Our most honest proving ground is our engineering teams. Before bringing Argon to developers in Antigravity, we put it to work inside Google. Today, over 100K users across Alphabet rely on Argon inside our internal version of Antigravity each month to solve complex production problems across our codebases. Over a four-week period, we have seen a 35% increase in agentic code, improving not just developer velocity, but code quality with a 30% decrease in post-submit rollbacks. Here are a few ways teams across Alphabet have been putting Argon in Antigravity to work on our hardest engineering challenges in products you love: YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms. Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues. Operating at Google-scale forced us to build Antigravity to be enterprise-ready from Day 1, transforming our day-to-day development across Google. By streamlining routine tasks that every enterprise development team faces, from refactoring legacy codebases to automating test coverage and resolving build breakages, Argon is freeing engineers to focus on higher-level architecture and product innovation: Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left. Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work. Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes. Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster. We are excited to provide our Gemini for business customers the same day-to-day acceleration that we’ve been seeing with Antigravity. Argon across disciplines One of the most encouraging things we’ve observed internally is how quickly teams outside core software engineering have adapted Argon in Antigravity for their own use cases. Monthly active usage outside of core engineering is soaring, with over half of Cloud sales, almost half of finance, and over a third of business and operations Googlers using Antigravity. Plugins, skills, and MCP integrations make it straightforward to connect the agent to specialized data sources and workflows. Using these customizations with Argon makes it easier to integrate with deep verticalized work, such as: Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review. Resolving a data dashboard outage: A TPM (Technical Program Manager) used Argon in Antigravity to autonomously resolve a critical P0 data center dashboard outage that had stalled for over four months. Without needing dedicated engineering support, the TPM diagnosed deep cross-stack database failures and landed a 3,200-line pipeline overhaul, restoring real-time visibility in just a few days. Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead. Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work. Getting started Argon is rolling out starting today in the Google Antigravity desktop app and CLI for Google AI Ultra subscribers , eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions , and in the API in Gemini platform. Update to the latest version of Antigravity to try it on your most complex workflows. We’d love to hear what you build and where we can make the experience better. candidates.title: Mix, Don’t Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings
candidates.author: Apple Machine Learning Research
candidates.summarizationContent: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing content type paper published October 2026 Mix, Don’t Tune: Bilingual Pre-Training Outperforms Hyperparameter Search in Data-Constrained Settings Authors Paul Jeha†**, Anastasiia Sedova, Louis Béthune, Skyler Seto, Jes Frellsen†‡, Pierre Ablin‡, Natalie Schluter‡ View publication Copy Bibtex For most languages of the world, language model pre-training operates in a data-constrained regime where models must repeat their training data many times, degrading generalization. Two remedies exist: aggressive hyperparameter tuning such as high weight decay, and mixing in data from a high-resource auxiliary language to directly aid the low-resource target. While hyperparameter tuning regularizes the model by shrinking weights to restrict network capacity, auxiliary data mixing uses a tunable mixing ratio to expand the training distribution and diversify the training signal with new knowledge. Both offer a principled way to improve training in a data-constrained domain. We compare these levers systematically across four model scales from 150M to 1.43B parameters, using Arabic as the low-resource target and English as the auxiliary, over approximately 1000 pre-training runs. Three findings emerge. First, mixing yields larger improvements than hyperparameter tuning on both validation loss and downstream task accuracy, and the gap grows with model size. Second, we quantify how much mixing helps: it boosts performance by an amount equivalent to 2–3× the unique target data on validation loss and 2–13× on downstream task accuracy, with the gain scaling steeply with model size. Third, this divergence reveals that target-language validation loss systematically underestimates mixing’s value. Mixing regularizes by diversifying the training signal and contributes knowledge the repeated target corpus cannot supply; validation loss captures only the first effect. Our practical recommendations are: mix in a high-resource language, prioritize the mixing ratio over hyperparameter tuning, and transfer hyperparameters from a small proxy model via μP. † DTU ‡ Equal senior authorship ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. Completed Hyperparameter Transfer across Modules, Width, Depth, Batch and Duration February 13, 2026 research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICLR Hyperparameter tuning can dramatically impact training stability and final performance of large-scale models. Recent works on neural network parameterisations, such as μP, have enabled transfer of optimal global hyperparameters across model sizes. These works propose an empirical practice of search for optimal global base hyperparameters at a small model size, and transfer to a large size. We extend these works in two key ways. To handle scaling… Read more Scaling Laws for Forgetting During Finetuning with Pretraining Data Injection June 20, 2025 research area Methods and Algorithms conference ICML A widespread strategy for obtaining a language model that performs well in a target domain is to fine-tune it by training it to do unsupervised next-token prediction on data from that domain. Fine-tuning presents two challenges: i) if the amount of target data is limited, as is the case in most practical applications, the model will quickly overfit, and ii) the model will drift away from the original model and forget the pre-training… Read more Discover opportunities in Machine Learning.
