candidates.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
candidates.author: Anthropic
candidates.summarizationContent: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard. As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones. The typical setup for scaling git checkouts. Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like? Principles for agent-scale source control With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling , so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are: Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it. Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally. A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control. Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed. Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem. The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads. How Scion works It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle. Data structures In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, 1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly. The shape of a changeset in Scion. This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets. A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents. This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search. Scaling Scion A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner. Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own. Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want. In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed. The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system. Scion’s checkout architecture. Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs. What we learned building Scion We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it. Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures. Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026. What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like. Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future. Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code. We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day. Observed performance improvements on native Scion repos. We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes. A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison. We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them. Contributing to the wider ecosystem We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case. Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities. Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful. However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well. Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential. Acknowledgements Written by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique. Footnotes Storing changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.

candidates.title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
candidates.author: Luca Zancato
candidates.summarizationContent: Machine learning Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch? “Priming” reuses pretrained Transformer weights to build models with more efficient architectures at less than 1% of the original training cost and with throughputs up to twice as high. By Luca Zancato October 12, 2026 14 min read Share Share Copy link Email X LinkedIn Facebook Line Reddit QZone Sina Weibo WeChat WhatsApp 分享到微信 x Key takeaways A new AWS paper introduces priming, a method that reduces pretraining costs for hybrid architectures by over 99% by leveraging pretrained Transformer weights, saving trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. A 32-billion-parameter Gated KalmaNet (GKA)-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWS) even when SWA receives twice the memory budget, and GKA's variable-iteration mechanism enables 10% faster decoding with only ~1% accuracy loss. Was this answer helpful? AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “ Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers ,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A 32-billion-parameter hybrid model reaches each accuracy threshold faster than an equivalently sized Transformer, converging to similar final accuracy in less wall clock time. The dataset is the AIME 2025 math competition benchmark (hard subset). Accuracy at time t is the fraction of rollouts for which a correct final answer has been produced by time t . A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. The Transformer outputs one token at a time, and each output token becomes a new input, so the context grows one token at a time as well. To save computation, the Transformer thus stores the key and value projections of each new input in a “KV cache”. Two kinds of memory layers: Eidetic versus fading The attention mechanism gives Transformers what we call eidetic memory : verbatim recall of every past token. The possibility of recalling over an LLM’s entire context window is what made in-context learning, long-document reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation possible. But it comes at a cost that scales with the number of input tokens. However, not all attention layers do the same job. Some perform long-range retrieval across tens of thousands of tokens. Others operate more locally, tracking the current clause, copying nearby tokens, and the like. The local ones don't need a growing cache: a compact, fixed-size summary of the past — what we call fading memory — suffices. Hybrid models mix both: attention layers (eidetic, growing cache) for the layers that need global recall and state space layers (fading, fixed size) for the rest. The result is a model with a reduced memory footprint that still has access to verbatim recall where it matters. Priming: Knowledge isn't locked to the architecture Exploring hybrids’ design space has been impractical because each hybrid configuration would normally require pretraining from scratch. Priming sidesteps this by reusing the stored knowledge in a pretrained Transformer's weights. Priming is possible because a Transformer is itself a special case of a state space realization . The outputs of both attention and SSM layers can be expressed as the result of multiplying the value sequence by a “mixing” matrix that decides how much each past token contributes to each current token. Attention computes the mixing matrix by multiplying the query and key matrices; an SSM produces a similar output through a recurrent state of fixed dimension that all past information must pass through. Priming takes advantage of this structural similarity: if an SSM with a fixed-dimensional state can produce a mixing matrix close enough to the attention layer's, the query, key, and value projections from the source Transformer can be reused as the SSM's own input projections, with only the SSM-specific parameters needing to be learned. Whether the approximation holds depends on whether the attention layer performs complex, long-range retrievals or simple, local operations. We distinguish between the two using a cheap empirical proxy: replace each layer with an SWA — which preserves only a fraction of the context — and measure the degradation. Layers that tolerate this substitution are natural candidates for SSM conversion: their mixing matrices don’t need to capture long-range relationships, so the state of an SSM can faithfully represent what they do. This proxy connects to a formal quantity from dynamical-systems theory, the Hankel rank of the layer's mixing matrix , which measures how much information must pass through the state bottleneck and therefore the minimum SSM state dimension required to realize the layer exactly. Priming proceeds in three stages: Layer selection: identify which layers can be faithfully compressed into a fixed-size state while retaining the rest as attention; Weight transfer and alignment: initialize SSM layers from the corresponding attention weights, then run a short distillation process aligning each SSM to the behavior of the layer it replaces; End-to-end adaptation: fine-tune the full hybrid model on next-token prediction, letting all layers coadapt. Priming begins with the use of a simple proxy (a sliding-window attention) to identify attention layers that largely operate locally. The weights of those layers are distilled into state-space-model (SSM) layers, which are then aligned with the behaviors of the layers they replace. Finally, the full hybrid model is fine-tuned on next-token prediction. The entire pipeline consumes less than 0.5% of the source model's pretraining token budget, and it works across Transformer families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model classes (dense or MoE), and scales (eight billion to 32 billion and more). With priming we can now explore the design space, the layer type, the hybrid ratio, and layer placement cheaply and systematically, because every variant starts from the same strong initialization and requires minimal training, compared to pretraining. A controlled comparison of fading-memory layers For instance, consider this question: given the same data, the same training budget, and the same ratio of eidetic to fading layers, which SSM layer works best in a hybrid model? In our paper , we evaluate three families of state space models, each representing a different approach to using a fixed-size state: Mamba-2 applies a uniform scalar decay to the entire state at each step, a running average that forgets everything at the same rate. When a new token arrives, it is written into the state, while all previous entries are uniformly attenuated. Mamba-2 is simple and efficient but indiscriminate. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) adds targeted updates on top of uniform decay. Rather than decaying everything uniformly, it can selectively erase the value previously associated with a specific key before writing the new one (the delta rule). This makes it more expressive than Mamba-2: it can revise a specific association without uniformly decaying the rest. Gated KalmaNet (GKA) goes further. Its erase direction depends not only on the current key but on statistics of all past keys , a history-aware update that accounts for the cumulative structure of everything the model has seen. The results of hybrid models using Mamba-2, GDN, and GKA state space models on four tasks. GKA generally outperforms GDN, which always outperforms Mamba-2, in line with theoretical predictions. The theoretical expressiveness hierarchy predicts the empirical one: GKA > GDN > Mamba-2. The gap widens on long-context reasoning, where compression quality matters most, and narrows on short-context tasks. Furthermore, at the 32-billion-parameter (32B) scale, hybrid GKA is within 1% of its source Transformer trained on the same data, despite requiring half the KV cache at inference. Fading memory beats verbatim windowed memory An interesting finding in our study comes from a direct comparison of hybrid models using SSM layers and those using sliding-window attention (SWA), which retain a fixed window of recent tokens verbatim rather than compressing the past into a state. One might expect that verbatim recall, even over a limited window, would outperform lossy compression. After all, no information is lost within the sliding window’s range. And stacking multiple SWA layers increases the “receptive field” of the end-to-end model. Instead, every SSM-based hybrid we tested outperformed the corresponding SWA hybrid on long-context benchmarks, even when the window gets two to four times as much memory as the state. Hybrid models using lossy context summaries (orange) consistently outperformed hybrid models using sliding context windows (teal) . A runtime knob for speed versus accuracy: Variable computation at inference time GKA has a property that neither Mamba-2 nor GDN offers: variable test-time computation. Mamba-2 and GDN have the same computation budget for every input token, regardless of its content. GKA, by contrast, solves a regression problem iteratively, and the iteration count is adjustable at serving time without retraining. The Gated KalmaNet (GKA) accuracy-speed frontier, at four different context lengths. Geometric shapes indicate different numbers of iterations on a regression problem. In practice, serving GKA at 10 iterations instead of its usual 30 sacrifices roughly 1% of its accuracy on AIME 2025 while delivering 10% faster decoding. A single trained model can serve multiple points on the speed-accuracy frontier, so model providers can offer different latency tiers without maintaining separate model variants. This connects to a principle we have discussed in earlier work: intelligence is the ability to allocate effort commensurate with difficulty . GKA's variable-computation mechanism is an architectural embodiment of this principle: a deployment that demands speed can run fewer iterations, while one that demands accuracy can run more. Faster reasoning, not just faster tokens Raw per-token throughput tells only part of the story. A model that is cheaper per token can still be slower end to end if its reasoning is weaker and it needs more tokens to compensate. The deployment-relevant question is how much more rapidly, in wall clock terms, the hybrid reaches a target accuracy. We measured this on AIME 2025, a challenging math competition benchmark, comparing our GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B-Reasoner against the source Qwen3-32B trained on the same reasoning recipe. Both models generate similar-length thinking traces (a median of about 14,000 tokens on the full set, 28,000 on the hardest problems) — that is, they produce equally in-depth responses — but the hybrid has a much higher throughput. At realistic concurrency levels, where the Transformer's KV cache saturates GPU memory, the hybrid reaches target accuracy thresholds 1.2 to 1.4 times as quickly on the full benchmark and up to 1.6 times as quickly on the hardest problems. This is a consequence of the SSM layers' fixed-size state, which roughly halves the per-sequence memory footprint, enabling more concurrent operations on the same hardware. Decode throughput speedup of GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B over the source Transformer as a function of context length. Replacing half the attention layers with a fixed-size SSM state roughly halves the size of the KV cache, yielding up to 2.06 times the throughput at a context length of 128,000 tokens. Lowering the number of GKA solver iterations from 30 to 10 at serving time (no retraining necessary) trades a small accuracy margin for additional throughput. The throughput advantage grows with context length: 1.50× at 16K tokens, scaling to 2.06× at 128K for the 32B model (GKA at 10 iterations). With the 8B parameter models, the gains are even greater: 1.94× at 16K to 2.29× at 128K. At long context, KV cache reads dominate the forward pass through the Transformer, and halving the cache roughly doubles the effective batch size at memory saturation. This has implications beyond inference serving. In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pipelines, throughput gates how rapidly the policy generates correct trajectories. The hybrid's advantage translates directly to a 20% to 100% increase in RL training data rate at a fixed GPU budget. Reasoning accuracy of GKA-primed hybrid models versus source Qwen3 Transformer models across five benchmarks at eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scale. Primed hybrid models match their source Transformers in quality at half the memory, and they decode faster. At eight billion parameters, the GKA hybrid uniformly outperforms its GDN counterpart, consistent with the theoretical expressiveness hierarchy GKA > GDN. Beyond the training window: Context extension with state composition Our primed hybrids natively support 128,000 tokens. But agent sessions, codebases, and long legal documents routinely exceed that. Extending context further would normally require another round of continued pretraining on curated data. Can the hybrid architecture itself generalize to longer contexts without additional training ? Existing training-free methods for expanding the context window fall into two classes: those for pure Transformers (positional-embedding rescaling schemes like YaRN) and those for pure SSMs, such as our PICASO , which we presented last year at the International Conference on Learning Representations ( ICLR ). Neither addresses the hybrid setting, where KV caches and recurrent states must be reconciled jointly. In our new arXiv paper , we describe a method of extending hybrid models’ context beyond their native limits without training. The procedure is simple: partition a long input into chunks shorter than the native context length and prepend a shared prefix to each chunk; process all chunks independently in parallel; concatenate the KV caches across chunks while merging the SSM states via the weighted-averaging scheme we introduced in our PICASO paper . State composition for hybrid models. Long inputs are partitioned into chunks at the native context length and processed independently. KV caches are concatenated, while SSM states are merged via the weighted-averaging scheme we proposed in our PICASO paper . This approach enables us to extend the context length of our primed hybrid models from 128K to 256K tokens while preserving substantial accuracy on both retrieval (RULER NIAH) and reasoning (BABILong) tasks at lengths the model was never trained on. In our experiments we show that hybrid state composition preserves the SSM expressivity hierarchy (GKA > GDN > Mamba-2). The hybrid design space is now open All artifacts discussed in this blog are released under the Apache 2.0 License in our Hybrid Model Factory on GitHub and our model zoo on HuggingFace: A collection of primed hybrids for long-context reasoning and instruction following (8B and 32B); The priming training code; Point-to-point sequence parallelism algorithms for SSM layers (up to 2.3 times as fast as all-to-all-based alternatives at multinode scale); Universal sequence parallelism for prototyping novel layers on long sequences without custom kernels or distributed-training expertise; Optimized Triton kernels for GKA decoding and training; A vLLM serving plugin supporting primed hybrid architectures with continuous batching, chunked prefill, and tensor parallelism for inference deployment at scale. If you serve long-context workloads, the 32B GKA reasoning model with the vLLM plugin gives you higher throughput with no quality loss on long context reasoning tasks. If you're scaling RL post-training, the hybrid's throughput advantage means more correct rollouts per unit time at a fixed GPU budget, for faster policy iteration without changing your training recipe. If you're researching new architectures, priming lets you evaluate any layer type under controlled conditions at a fraction of the pretraining cost while starting from a strong initialization. The universal SP module means you don't need custom distributed kernels to train at long context. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class. Extending it to Llama, Mistral, or MoE models requires no algorithmic changes. We hope these tools enable the community to explore architectures beyond what we've tested and to develop new algorithms and training recipes for building scalable next-generation architectures for AI agents. For full details, see our paper, " Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers ". Code, models, and serving plugin are available on GitHub , and the models are also on Hugging Face . Research areas Machine learning Tags Network architectures Agentic AI About the Author Luca Zancato Luca Zancato is a senior applied scientist in Amazon Web Services' Fundamental Research organization.

candidates.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
candidates.author: alyssa
candidates.summarizationContent: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway. Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines. Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal. Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance. The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. Looking ahead StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available. candidates.title: How distributed inference keeps large AI models moving
candidates.author: Peter Hess
candidates.summarizationContent: When an AI model answers a question or completes a task, it performs inference, i.e., using a trained model to generate an output in response to some input. Doing that at scale, however, is more challenging than it sounds. Running a large language model on a GPU is one thing. Serving that model to thousands or even millions of people and AI agents at the same time is quite another. Requests arrive with different priorities and lengths, which have unique computing needs. Some users expect an immediate response to simple queries, while others submit large jobs that can run in the background. AI agent traffic adds a new pattern: Agents may send bursts of related requests, pause to call a tool, and then return with nearly the same context. Meanwhile, the system must make efficient use of expensive accelerators without creating long queues or repeatedly performing the same computations. This challenge resembles air traffic control. A busy airport cannot simply send each arriving aircraft to the first available runway. Controllers in the tower must account for the aircraft’s location, destination, size, and fuel needs, as well as the traffic already moving through the system. The challenge might be simple if all air traffic controllers had to do was keep every runway busy, but an airport isn’t a parking lot, and not every airplane can be treated the same way. Distributed inference plays a similar coordinating role for LLM inference, working a layer above model servers like vLLM and SGLang , where it orchestrates and optimizes real-world traffic. While those serving engines run models efficiently on individual servers, a distributed inference serving framework coordinates groups of model servers across a cluster. Its router can consider queue depth, cache availability, and server roles before deciding where a request should go. To understand how distributed inference works, we’ll look at six notable technical innovations—prefix-cache-aware routing, KV-cache offloading, flow control, batch inference optimization, prefill/decode disaggregation, and wide expert parallelism. We’ll also see how each comes together in llm-d, an open-source, Kubernetes-native inference framework. Prefix-cache-aware routing: Sending work where context already lives KV-cache offloading: Extending a model’s working memory Flow control: Deciding what moves and when Batch inference optimization: Filling spare capacity without clogging the system Prefill/decode disaggregation: Separating two different types of work Wide expert parallelism: Spreading a giant model across the cluster Coordinating the whole inference system Prefix-cache-aware routing: Sending work where context already lives When a language model reads a prompt, it produces an internal representation of the words and their relationships, storing much of this intermediate state in a key-value cache, or KV cache. If a later request begins with the same text, or even portions of the same text, the model may be able to reuse that stored computation rather than re-process the shared text. For example, if an existing prompt is “What is the capital of Kansas?” then later on you ask, “What is the capital of California?” the KV cache for the "what is the capital of" portion is reused. This opportunity arises frequently in real workloads. A chatbot receives the same system instructions at the beginning of every conversation. A coding assistant repeatedly examines the same repository. An AI agent may revisit a long record of previous steps while testing different solutions. In each case, much of the prompt remains unchanged from turn to turn. A conventional load balancer may send the next request to whichever server appears least busy, whether or not its cache contains the relevant context. As a result, the model must reread material that another server has already processed. Prefix-cache-aware routing instead asks two questions: Which server already holds the greatest portion of this prompt’s prefix, and which server has enough capacity to handle the request? The llm-d router uses cache information and operating conditions to score the available model servers and select a suitable destination. There is both an approximate implementation that includes a lightweight index of recent routing decisions, and a precise implementation based on actual token data and cache-state updates from model servers. If an aircraft already has its passengers, baggage, and ground crew waiting at one gate, sending the plane to another gate would introduce needless work. In the same way, a distributed inference system tries to send a request to the model server that already contains the required context. The payoff is less redundant prefill computation, lower latency, and greater throughput. In a recent demonstration from the team behind llm-d, prefix-aware routing captured 97% of the available reuse in the tested workload. More broadly, the technique is especially useful for agentic systems because their requests often share long instructions, source material, conversation histories, and tool outputs. llm-d was launched in May 2025 as a collaborative effort by founding members IBM Research, Red Hat, Google Cloud, NVIDIA, and CoreWeave. Several founding partners also took part from the start, including industry leaders like AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI, and academic supporters at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of Chicago. IBM Research, Red Hat, and Google Cloud continue to lead llm-d's development today, and its community of partners and contributors has grown considerably. In March 2026, the founders donated llm-d to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project, to further the mission of deploying inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud. KV-cache offloading: Extending a model’s working memory Cache-aware routing is most valuable when cached information remains available. The problem is that although accelerator memory is fast, its space can be quickly filled by long prompts, many concurrent users, and extended agent sessions. When space runs short, a model server may evict older KV-cache entries. If a later request needs that material, the model must calculate it again, wasting accelerator cycles rebuilding context that existed moments earlier. Distributed inference addresses this problem through KV-cache offloading . Rather than treating accelerator memory as the only place where cached context can live, it chooses an offloading target based on workload requirements. The most immediately useful entries can remain in high-bandwidth accelerator memory, while other entries can move to larger but slower tiers such as CPU memory, local solid-state storage, or a shared file system. A cache index tracks what is stored and where, allowing the routing layer to incorporate offloaded data into its decisions. Retrieving cached information from CPU memory or storage is slower than reading it directly from accelerator memory, but it is much faster and less expensive than recomputing the entire prompt. Offloading therefore expands the system’s effective cache capacity beyond the physical memory available on its accelerators. This matters most for workloads with long, reusable contexts and many simultaneous sessions. In the same llm-d demonstration mentioned in the previous section, GPU memory supplied about 90% to 92% of reusable prefill prefixes for 128 concurrent requests, with CPU offloading helping to preserve prefixes beyond GPU capacity. In another demonstration , CPU offloading helped the system sustain high throughput and low time to first token across a long, agent-driven benchmark. Because offloading runs during prefill and writes to slower tiers happen asynchronously, these gains come without slowing token generation. Flow control: Deciding what moves and when Routing answers where a request should go. But under load, a system also has to decide which requests move first — and which ones wait. When a burst of traffic arrives at once, treating every request identically means a latency-sensitive query can end up stuck behind a backlog of lower-priority work. Air traffic controllers face the same problem and solve it with traffic flow management. When demand exceeds capacity, they meter departures, sequence arrivals, and hold lower-priority traffic on the ground so that a full airliner on final approach isn't delayed behind a cargo run that could just as easily wait a few minutes. Distributed inference needs the same discipline. llm-d's flow control governs how requests are admitted and ordered as they enter the system, enforcing fairness across users and priority across workloads. Latency-sensitive interactive traffic can be protected, while bursty or deferrable work is paced to fit the capacity that remains. This keeps a single noisy tenant or a sudden surge of agent activity from degrading response times for everyone else. This becomes especially important with agentic traffic, which is uneven by nature: An agent may sit idle, then fire a burst of related requests, then pause to call a tool. Flow control absorbs that irregularity, smoothing bursts into an orderly stream rather than letting them overwhelm the cluster. Batch inference optimization: Filling spare capacity without clogging the system Not every inference request needs an immediate answer. Research evaluations, document processing, synthetic-data generation, and large-scale testing may involve thousands or millions of prompts that can be completed over time. These batch jobs can improve hardware utilization by using capacity that might otherwise sit idle, like routing air freight to unused runways. Handled poorly, batch jobs can flood the system and delay interactive traffic. A batch workload should not make a person wait unnecessarily for a coding assistant or customer-service response. llm-d supports batch and offline inference through two complementary components. A Batch Gateway provides an OpenAI-compatible interface for submitting, tracking, and managing batch inference jobs. An asynchronous processor can pull individual requests from message queues, including Redis and Google Pub/Sub, and dispatch them to the llm-d router. This design separates job management from request placement. The batch layer determines how work enters the system, while the router still decides where each individual request should run. Batch jobs rely on flow control to pace their entry according to current load rather than releasing an entire job into the cluster at once. The result is faster batch processing, as well as a more orderly use of shared infrastructure. Organizations can keep accelerators productive while protecting the responsiveness of higher-priority applications. Prefill/decode disaggregation: Separating two different types of work Generating an LLM response involves two computational phases. During prefill, a model processes the input prompt and builds the KV cache. This phase can involve large amounts of parallel computation, particularly when a prompt contains tens of thousands of tokens. During decode, the model generates the response one token at a time. Decode is sequential and highly sensitive to memory access and communication delays, placing different demands on the hardware than prefill. A conventional serving system may run both phases on the same group of accelerators, which simplifies deployment but creates competition between dissimilar workloads. A large prefill job can interrupt or delay steady token generation, while hardware configured for responsive decoding may be a poor fit for processing very long prompts. Prefill/decode disaggregation allows a distributed inference system to assign the phases to specialized workers and scale them independently. The router selects a prefill endpoint and a decode endpoint, then coordinates the transfer of the resulting KV-cache state between them. This separation makes the infrastructure more adaptable. A workload dominated by long documents may require more prefill capacity. A service supporting many active conversations may need more decode capacity. Instead of expanding the entire serving cluster, operators can add resources where the pressure actually exists. Disaggregation also reduces interference between the phases. Prompt processing can be optimized for throughput, while generation can be optimized for the consistent delivery of tokens. Prefill/decode disaggregation allows the two phases to scale independently, improving efficiency for variable workloads. Wide expert parallelism: Spreading a giant model across the cluster Some of today’s largest language models use a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture. Instead of applying every part of the model to every token, an MoE model contains many specialized neural networks, called experts. A routing mechanism selects only a small subset of experts for each token. This approach reduces the amount of computation required for each request, but it does not eliminate the need to store the model’s full set of weights. Large MoE models can require hundreds of gigabytes of memory just to hold all their weights, leaving less accelerator memory available for the KV cache and other parts of inference. Traditional tensor parallelism addresses the memory problem by dividing individual model operations across several GPUs, which can require frequent communication among the GPUs. For models using certain attention mechanisms, it may also create multiple copies of the same KV-cache data, reducing the capacity available for long contexts and concurrent users. Wide expert parallelism takes a different approach. It distributes the model’s experts across GPUs and, when necessary, across physical servers. When the model determines which experts should process a token, the system sends that token only to the GPUs holding the selected experts. Those experts perform their calculations, and the results return to the original processing path. Because this communication is sparse, the GPUs exchange the information needed for the selected experts rather than continuously synchronizing every model operation. In air traffic terms, the system does not require every specialist at the airport to work on every aircraft. It directs each task to the small number of specialists it actually needs. Memory efficiency is a significant advantage of this technique. Spreading expert weights across a wider group of accelerators leaves more memory on each GPU for the KV cache. The effect can be substantial. In a demonstration this year from IBM and Red Hat, the wide layout stored about 65.1 GiB of expert weights per GPU, compared with 89.5 GiB in the tensor-parallel layout examined. On the same hardware, the wide configurations provided between three and nine times as much KV-cache capacity, depending on the topology. In this way, wide expert parallelism helps distributed inference systems like llm-d serve extremely large MoE models while preserving room for long prompts and many active sessions. It also complements prefill/decode disaggregation: One divides inference by phase, while the other distributes the model’s experts across the cluster. Used together, the two allow llm-d to match the organization of the hardware more closely to the structure of the model and the demands of the workload. Coordinating the whole inference system As with an airport’s system of air traffic controllers, ground crews, and flight crews, each element is valuable on its own but can’t run the operation on its own. Prefix-cache-aware routing identifies where reusable context resides. KV-cache offloading preserves more of that context across a hierarchy of memory and storage. Flow control manages incoming requests to maintain capacity for simultaneous users. Batch inference controls how large volumes of background work enter the system. Prefill/decode disaggregation sends fundamentally different phases of inference to resources suited to each one. And wide expert parallelism physically distributes large models across clusters to make the best use of accelerator memory. Together, they turn LLM serving from a collection of isolated model servers into a coordinated and distributed system. That distinction becomes increasingly important as AI moves beyond simple chat and toward agents that maintain long contexts, call tools, collaborate with other agents, and generate irregular bursts of traffic. The air traffic control analogy only goes so far, but its central lesson holds: Performance depends on coordination, not just raw capacity. Building more runways does not automatically make an airport efficient, and adding more accelerators does not automatically make inference fast or affordable. The system also needs to know where work should go, what can be reused, which tasks can wait, and which resources are best suited to each stage. That is the role distributed inference is designed to fill.

candidates.title: Self-Compacting Language Model Agents
candidates.author: Apple Machine Learning Research
candidates.summarizationContent: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference NeurIPS content type paper published October 2026 Self-Compacting Language Model Agents Authors Tianjian Li†, Jingyu Zhang†, William Jurayj†, Xi Wang†, Chuanyang Jin†, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Eric Nalisnick†, Daniel Khashabi† View publication Copy Bibtex Long agent traces composed of chains of thought and tool calls accumulate stale content that anchor subsequent generations, and eventually outgrow the context window. Existing scaffolds mitigate it with fixed-interval compaction triggered at a token threshold. Such triggers pay no heed to trajectory structure, risking discard of partial results mid-derivation or mid-search. We propose SELFCOMPACT, a scaffold that allows the model itself to decide when and how to compact. Specifically, it pairs two inference-time elements: (i) a compaction tool the model invokes to summarize the accumulated context, and (ii) a lightweight rubric specifying when to fire (a sub-task has resolved, or the trajectory is converging) and when to suppress (mid-derivation, or when stuck). Both are needed. The tool alone is unevenly used across open-weight models, often invoked at unhelpful moments or not at all; the rubric alone cannot act. Together, they elicit effective adaptive compaction without any fine-tuning or external supervision. We present empirical results on six benchmarks (competitive math and agentic search) and seven models. Our results show that SELFCOMPACT matches or exceeds fixed-interval summarization at a fraction of the token cost, improving over a no-summarization baseline by up to 18.1 points on math and 5–9 points on agentic search at 30–70% lower per-question cost. Our results expose a meta-cognitive gap: although unprompted models cannot reliably tell when their own context is rotting, a lightweight rubric closes this gap, reframing when to compact as a capability that scaffolds can supply without training. † Johns Hopkins University Related readings and updates. RISED: Rubrics for Agentic Multi-Environment Selection and Self-Distillation October 6, 2026 research area Data Science and Annotation , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection.
